Before the orders of the day are proceeded with, I wish to call the attention of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) to a communication that I have received from a prominent gentleman in my riding, and which I beg leave to read. It is dated 23rd of this month.
Dear Mr. Lennox,-My object in writing you is to lay before you certain facts in connection with the immigration department at St. John, N.B.
I came out from England on the Allan Line steamer ' Corsican ' recently, landing at St. John, N.B., on Saturday evening, April 2nd. The vessel docked at 6 or a few minutes before 6 o'clock that evening, with about 600 passengers on board. The Allan Company had two special trains ready to take us to Montreal, had all the passengers' baggage on deck ready to land, had arranged to have the customs officials on hand to pass the baggage, when we were told that the immigration agent would not permit any passengers to land that night, and so far as I could learn from the captain of the ' Corsican,' without any special reason. We all had to remain on board that night, as not a passenger was permitted to land, and we did not get away from St. John until 3.30 on Sunday afternoon, causing much annoyance and inconvenience to all the passengers.
You would oblige me very much if you would lay this matter before the proper officials at Ottawa.

I lay this before the minister with the hope that he will make inquiries into the subject of the complaint as soon as convenient.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will be glad to take up the matter of the letter my hon. friend has read. Of course, we desire to avoid delay and inconvenience as much as possible, but it may be that in the present rush when there are so many ships coming in and so many people to handle, the difficulty was not avoidable. I will be glad to go into the matter fully. Certainly I can assure my hon. friend that there is every desire on the _ part of the department to redress any grievances that may occur.
I will hand the letter over to the minister.

I have the following communication to make to the House:
The Clerk of the House having requested, for the reasons set forth in his communication to me dated the 25th instant, copy of which is hereto appended, the withdrawal of my recommendation respecting a proposed reorganization of the staff of the House of Commons, laid upon the table of the House on the 6th instant. I hereby withdraw the same in order that the subject may be further considered.

Mr. KING moved the third reading of Bill (No. 101) to provide for the investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers which may enhance prices or restrict competition to the detriment of consumers.

I would like to say with regard to this Bill, that having looked over it somewhat carefully. I have reached the conclusion that it will prove to be a gold brick in so far as it will give any relief from combines under the law. This Bill contemplates, first, affidavits to be examined by a judge of six parties that they are affected by some combine injuriously. Then, provided the judge is satisfied that there is prima facie evidence, he grants permission to have a board of inquiry named. That board holds an inquiry, and provided the board reaches the conclusion that there are evidences to satisfy them that a combine exists, then, I take it, the case is allowed to stand for the time being. They decide^ that a combine exists, but if the parties interested continue to carry on their work, then the penalties under this Act may be imposed, but they are not imposed, I understand, until an inquiry is made before a judge, and an indictment is framed which has to be inquired into by some court. But it does not appear to me very evident what court it is, whether it is 253
the Exchequer or any other court. But this indictment must take place before any other inquiry or trial can be proceeded with. Then that court may impose a fine, and I imagine that if the court imposes a fine the penalties of the Act can be enforced as well as penalties under the criminal law. But after that is done, I imagine that the individual or combine has a right to appeal. Now the natural course will be that they will make their appeal to the court of appeal, and a combine is not likely to give up its rights so easily where such large interests are involved. The case will continue before that court of appeal until the court disposes of it. Suppose that the conviction is sustained, then the combine may go to the Supreme Court and fight it out there.; and suppose that the conviction is sustained by the Supreme Court, the combine may take it to the Privy Council. Now, after this is all done, justice may be meted out. But what will be the result? The case has got to traverse at least six courts before there is any infliction of a penalty that is collectable. Now, are there six men to be found in Canada who will be innocent enough to undertake a prosecution under these circumstances?
Another feature which attracted my attention is that when you come before the first court, the prosecution has got to take place under the same law that has been on the statute-books for years, and under which it has been declared that no prosecution can be successfully carried on with the object of getting a verdict. That statement has been made in this House, and also toy the late Attorney General of the province of Ontario, Sir Oliver Mowat, a prosecution under this case 'has got to toe made under exactly the same law. Then what is the remedy? The remedy is one or two things, or both. One is that if the article dealt with is an article upon which there is a customs duty, the Governor in Council may reduce the duty to whatever extent they see fit. Or, on the other hand, a penalty may be imposed that is provided under the criminal law. Now I say one or both things may be done. But we have had the same law on the statute-books since 1899, providing that the same thing might be done, and we have had no prosecution. Why? Because it has been said bv eminent lawyers who have looked into lit, and by that very high authority, Sir Oliver Mowat, that no prosecution can successfully be carried on under that law; and yet this is just exactly the same law that has been declared to be unworkable, and under which a prosecution could not successfully be sustained. If you look over the whole ground you can come to but one conclusion and that is that this Act is only a gold brick to the people, making them



believe that some new device has been introduced whereby they may get justice and whereby that which is a combine to the detriment of the consumer or the producer may be punished. I am sure that the law will remain on the statute-book for years to come and no prosecution practically will take place under it. I need not say anything with regard to the trouble, annoyance, delay and everything else that are going to result, or as to who will pav the expense, because it is so unworkable that it seems to me that it is little less than a straw. It reminds me very much of the story of the German who traded horses. When he was asked if he had any fault, to which he Teplied, no except some trifling ones of no account. After the deal was completed, the new owner said what are those trifling faults, to which he replied- one that the horse was hard to catch and the other that was no good when he was not caught. The people have got this Bill and it is no good when they have got it.
Mr. Speaker, I want to draw the attention of the House foT a moment or two to a paragraph that I find in the Winnipeg ' Tribune ' on the cement merger.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

The question is on the third reading of this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Has my hon. friend reference to this Bill ?
Yes.
I understood that the hon. gentleman wanted to' put a question.

No, it is in reference to combines that I want to speak. In the early part of the session I drew the attention of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) to the effect that the cement merger was likely to have in increasing the cost of cement in the province of Manitoba and throughout the Dominion. I hold in my hand the Winnipeg ' Tribune ' of the 23rd instant, a paper that hon. gentlemen on the opposite side used to swear by. It is as follows :

The advocates of high protective tariff would do well to consider the effect of high duty in the case of cement.
In the course of last year about 400,000 barrels of cement passed through Winnipeg, and roughly speaking, about half of this quantity was used in Winnipeg, or for Winnipeg works. In view of the inordinate amount of building in the city and such works as the new bridges and the power plant at Pointe du Bois, which will alone require at least sixty or seventy thousand barrels, it is more than fair to assume that at least the same quantity will be required by Winnipeg ratepayers this year, namely, 200,000 barrels.
How much more will this amount cost this Mr. SPEOULE.
year than last? At the present time contractors in the city are paying $2.40 a barrel for the same grade of cement as they were purchasing as low as $1.80 last year before the merger was formed, which was brought into existence by the high protective tariff- an advance of 60 cents. This means that if this rate is maintained-and there is no reason for supposing anything else-Winnipeg alone will pay $120,000 more for its cement than last year. At the present time the merger is selling cement at from 10 to- 15 cents a barrel less than the price at which it can be brought in from the United States. They have protection of from 51 to 52 cents per barrel, which is prohibitive. A barrel of cement can be sold at the factory anywhere in Ontario, in round figures, at $1 a barrel. The duty is, therefore, over 50 per cent.
If the duty were reduced to 30 * per cent, which is the average charge on manufactured goods, then it would be possible for the consumer of Manitoba to import their cement from the United States, if the Canadian merger did not make a fair price.
I would like to emphasize what I said in an earlier part of the session when I had the assurance of tire Minister of Finance at that time that a Bill was under way which would deal with this matter. It is very important to the western country. I may say that in all our great structures today due perhaps to the increased cost of lumber, we are using cement very largely arid while the ' Tribune ' estimates that 400,000 barrels of cement will pass through Winnipeg this year over different lines, I think it would be safe to say that a far larger quantity of cement will have to pass through Winnipeg to supply the needs of that growing country. I would like to ask the minister in charge of this Bill if he intends to make an investigation and take such proceedings as to cause the meTger to do what is fair with the people in the west. The suggestion of the ' Tribune ' that the protection should be reduced on this article, I think, is a very fair and wise one. I think that when we find that mergers are causing an increase in the cost of commodities which they are producing which is unfair to the consumer, the government should reduce or take off the duty altogether if it is necessary to force the combines to give the people the product, whatever it may be, at reasonable price. There is no doubt about this cement merger being a serious drawback to the west. You could get cement 'at $1.80 last year; now it is $2.40 a barrel. That is brought about, I am satisfied, 'by the merger, and the government ought to take immediate action to protect the consumer in this matter.

Mr. Speaker, before the Bill is read a third time I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. King) a question in connection with clause 5. It says :

Where six or more persons are of opinion that a combine exists, and that prices have been enhanced or competition restricted by reason of such combine, to the detriment of consumers, such persons may make an application to a judge for an order directing an investigation into such alleged combine.
In connection with that application, made by such six persons, there will be considerable expense. There will have to be legal advice and quite a lot of expense in connection with it and the question I would like to ask the Minister of Labour is whether the government intend to assume that expense. I may say that if they do not the utility of the bill is entirely destroyed. I would like an answer to that question before the bill is read a third time.

Mr. Speaker, the hon member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), in all his speaking on this Bill, has, I think, kept too largely in mind the enactments passed with which he has had to do. He seems to forget that in this measure particular stress is not laid on the prosecution side, but that it is rather to the investigation feature that the government look for the chief advantage to be derived. The hon. member for East Grey has pointed out that there may be half a dozen different stages through which persons adversely affected by a combine may have to go before they get the result which they would like to get in the way of a remedy. Let me say in the first place that there are *certain classes of industrial evils in regard to which publicity is more effective than penalty and therefore it is not in the penalty (side of this measure that the remedy will lie so much as in the fear and consequence of the publicity which will be given to the wrongful doings of particular combines.
If that is so how are you going to benefit from examinations in private ?

The hon. gentleman mentions that owing to the fact that some preliminary examinations have to take place this feature in part is offset. If the government had brought in a measure which would permit of the examination of any business of this country at the request of any individual without some form of preliminary examination to ascertain whether or not there were prima facie grounds for saying that a combine did exist and was operating adversely to the public the government would have been open to censure for so doing. The extent of the preliminary examination is not considerable. It is simply to enable the judge who is accustomed to dealing with evidence and to sizing up situations to say whether or 253i
not sufficient evidence has been obtained to warrant a further examination taking place. Now, as to the opportunity which the measure affords for full investigation and as to the machinery of the measure, I doubt if it would be possible to devise a board better calculated to get at the facts with regard to industrial conditions than a board which is composed of a person appointed by those who feel that they have a grievance, a person appointed by those who are complained against and a judge who is accustomed to dealing with matters of inquiry and who will hold the balance evenly between those two.
That is the effective machinery for getting at the facts that this measure provides The hon. member would have us believe that after this investigation the only remedy would be through a criminal prosecution. But the hon. gentleman has failed to recognize the power which at present exists in the Governor in Council to remove customs duties when it appears that a combine has taken advantage of the protection which the tariff affords, to raise prices, and that whereas up to the present that power could only be exercised as the result of a judicial inquiry, carried on at the expense ,of private parties, under the present legislation that step can be taken as the result of the investigation by one of the boards. All expenses will now be met 'by the government instead of by the private parties as formerly, and it is because the expense has heretofore been on the private parties that the existing legislation lias not achieved the results expected from it. Many a group of consumers have hesitated to set the existing law in motion, in the first place, because they were unwilling to charge another group of citizens with being criminals, and because, in the second place, they were unwilling to incur the large cost which such an investigation in the public interest would entail. This legislation will remove these objections. The purpose of the preliminary examination under this Bill is simply to put aside that class of actions which might be taken if it were left to any one on any ground whatever to start an inquiry against a particular concern, and to secure the limiting of examinations under this Bill to cases that reallv appear to be in the public interest.
How can you inflict the penalty?
I will mention two or three different ways in which a penalty may be imposed.
I mean the penalty provided in the Bill.

Assuming an inquiry has taken place into some alleged combine, and

during the course of the examination it is made plain to the general public that a group of men have taken advantage of the protection afforded by the tariff to unduly enhance prices, the government as a result of a finding by the hoard to that effect may remove the customs duty and thereby lower the price of that article to the whole body of consumers, and that brings about what is primarily desired, namely, relief to the consumers. The question as to whether the parties concerned in the combine shall be punished criminally is secondary in importance to the relief which the public needs.
Suppose it was an article on which there was no tariff?
Let us assume that it is a patented article.
Suppose there is a combine by which the farmer, the producer, does not get a fair price for his produce?

Perhaps the hon. member will allow me to take in their order the different forms of redress which the measure affords. A kind of combine under which the public to-day is suffering, judging by the representations made, is in the case of a patented article which is needed in manufacturing, and the concern owning it refuses to sell the patented article except on conditions which are in restraint of trade, such as binding the purchaser to purchase all other .articles from the same concern that holds the patent. Here is a case of a person receiving a monopoly from the .state, and having received that monopoly in the public interest taking advantage of the monopoly which the state has given him to use it against the general interest of consumers. If the board finds that such a thins? exists, power is given under the Act to see that that patent is revoked. I might mention a case that came under my notice in my own riding. We have in the town of Berlin a first-class manufacturing concern which produces cabinets for phonographs at a price of something like $125 each. The producer of the cabinet has no records, and I am informed that the dealers all over the country are refusing to sell his cabinet because they are unable ito get the records of other phonograph companies if they sell .any other than the cabinets which these phonograph companies make, and I am told that their cabinets are sold at double the .price which the Canadian cabinet is sold for. This firm'c cabinets are manufactured in Canada and the others are manufactured in the United States. A case of that kind, if proven, would afford the strongest reason why the state would be justified in taking the .patent on records away from the people who hold it if they undertake to use it as Mr. MACKENZIE KING.
against the Canadian manufacturer who is producing another article.
Is it proposed to regulate the record peoDle by the Patent Act or by this legislation.
This legislation will point the way to the form of redress which is necessary.
Does the minister not think that the use of the Patent Act itself as in Germany and other European countries would be more effective than anything else in regulating these combines?

In the present Bill some features of the Patent Act have been extended in the direction in which my hon. friend indicates. We are legislating by this measure to bring .the patent law into accord with some of the features of the German Patent Act. Again, you may have cases such as you had a few years ago when it was shown that two of the tobacco companies operating in the United States were requiring the dealers in Canada, to sell only the article they were putting on the market to the exclusion of all others. I think the American Tobacco company was one of these and there was another. The investigation showed that the producers and manufacturers of tobacco in this country were at a disadvantage in consequence of the monopolistic control which those_ two American concerns had over the business in this country. The present measure affords an opportunity of_ getting at the facts and letting in the light on whether a concern of that kind is acting in a monopolistic way here. If that were proven, then the government might cancel the license issued to such a firm by the Department of Inland Revenue for the sale of that commodity in Canada. Again, there might he a combine in the shipping business. If it were shown that a number of steamship companies receiving subsidies from this government were combining together to put up the ocean freight rates, and an investigation established this, it would he plain _ that the government would be justified in taking some action to see that the concerns which were receiving the subsidies did not take advantage of these subsidies to the detriment of "the public as a whole, and that the public should receive its rightful share of benefit from the steamship companies in virtue of the subsidies they were obtaining from the government.
While there is no immediate provision in the measure for the removal of subsidies granted, if an investigation went to show that some subsidized company were operating in that manner, there would be a strong reason why parliament, when it met, having the facts before .it, should take some action in the public interest.

I wish to get an answer to the question I put to the hon. minister. Where proceedings would be taken against the parties and you could impose the penalties of the law, upon what would those proceedings take place?

I have not come to that point yet. I am dealing with the hon. gentleman's assertion that this Act was a gold brick, and t-fiat it would only have any effect where the parties were proceeded against under the Criminal Code. I am endeavouring to point out that that i's only one and a very remote feature of the legislation, and that the remedies to which the government attach special importance in this measure are primarily those which are going to afford relief to the people suffering in virtue of these combines, and that secondarily attention will be paid to the penalizing of persons who persist in keeping up a combine against the public interest.
Will the Bill afford relief to the public against the insurance underwriters?
Perhaps I had better take up the questions in the order in which they are given.

What I want to know is will these punishments take place without the preliminary inquiry before the board. Will the government institute an inquiry before they will take action say with regard to patents, with regard to duties, with regard to subsidies or anything else? Will action be taken on the information brought out by the board, or will the government continue the inquiry further before they will inflict the punishment?

I am glad the hon. gentleman has asked that question because I think it will clear up the misunderstanding in his mind. It is on the finding of the board that the kind of action I have been mentioning will be taken. This could take place were there no penal clause at all. The portion of the measure to which my hon. friend is alluding is that which relates to combines which has been reported against as doing something contrary to the public interest, and which persist in doing that despite the findings of the board. In a case of that sort criminal proceedings may be taken. The findings of the board being before the public, there will be the strongest reason why the law should be set in motion against parties who are persisting in doing something against the public -interest, and the facts which have been brought out in evidence in an investigation of this kind may be used against them in a criminal action. That is where the investigating feature gives gome strength
to the Criminal Code in respect to the penalties now provided. Up to the present time the hon. gentleman says the criminal legislation has been in part useless in so far as that is true it is for the simple reason that there has been no way of ascertaining the full facts in advance; there has been no way of establishing that the parties proceeded against are really criminal; but if the board has reported that they are doing wrong, and if the combine persists in the teeth of a report of that sort in continuing a condition of affairs against the public interest, then the Criminal Code comes to have a significance much greater than it has at present, and there is the strongest reason for the prosecuting authorities to proceed against a combine of that sort under the Criminal Code.

If you commence a prosecution under the Criminal Code, are you not obliged to secure a conviction under the wording of the old law, under which it has been declared that you cannot secure a criminal conviction at present? That is the advice of every eminent counsel.

As against the advice of the very eminent counsel I will cite cases in which convictions have been obtained under the criminal law:
Wampole & Co. v. F. E. Karn Co., Limited -Contract-Sale of goods-agreement as to prices on re-sale-illegal combination or conspiracy unduly to enhance prices for medicinal preparations and lessen competition-refusal to enforce contract-Criminal Code, secs. 516, 520.
Plaintiff brought action before Clute, .T., for damages and injunction to restrain the breach of two contracts entered into between themselves and defendants, fixing price at which goods to be sold to retailers. Judgment held that agreements were breach of combines section of the Criminal Code.
That was not a criminal prosecution.
It was brought under sections 516 and 520 of the Criminal Code.

The hon. gentleman misunderstands. It was a case between two parties. The contract was held to be illegal because it was in breach of the criminal law of the country, but it was not a criminal prosecution.

The law to which the hon. member for East Grey was alluding was embodied in the sections of the Criminal Code which were introduced into this House by Mr. Clarke Wallace. It was under those sections that the case was brought. The point of the hon. member for East Grey was that the legislation was of no service.
It might be different if it were a question of sending the parties to jail.
That is the only case 1 ever heard anything about.
I am glad the honourable member admits this one, the hon. gentleman stated that there were none. But there were other cases. There was the case of the King vs. Elliott.

That was dropped.
That was the Brantford case.

That case was not dropped. There was a conviction. Then there was a case in the west 'against a lumber combine.
The King v. Clarke.-The defendant was charged with several offences under section 498 of the Criminal Code. The indictment (or charge) contained 12 counts relating to alleged agreements between the accused, Clarke, and certain lumber dealers to unduly limit facilities for supplying or dealing in lumber. The trial, which occupied 10 days, took place before Chief Justice Sifton without a jury, at Edmonton, in the sittings of the court in November, 1907, the accused being found guilty and sentenced to pay a fine of $500.
The accused appealed under Criminal Cede section 1012, and the appeal was heard before Scott, Harvey, Stuart and Beck, JJ., at Calgary, on July 8 to 15, 1908. The appeal was dismissed and conviction affirmed.
That is another case and I think I might possibly mention one or two others, but I do not wish to take up too much of the time of the House. However. I think from the citation, of the cases I have mentioned, the hon. member will see that even where the public do not have the facts before them, even where the parties who went into this prosecution had to risk the expense of the prosecution and had to make out their case, they were successful under the crim-Mr. KING.
ial code in bringing to time certain combines which was operating detrimentally to the public. Now, if he will consider how much easier it will be for a prosecution "to take place after an investigation has brought out all the facts, the hon. member will see wherein the penalty clause, if it is punishment he is looking for, where punishment is more likely to be secured in virtue of the penalties under this Act -and under the machinery which this Act provides. One of the difficulties has been to get the Attorneys Generals of the provinces to take action against combines and the reason of that has been that the public has not been aware of the facts. But does the hon. member suppose for a moment that if a board of inquiry had been inquiring into the facts of a particular combine and had brought in a report which in the strongest terms condemned that combine, the Attorney General in any province would refrain from proceeding under the criminal code, if it appeared that the combine continued in spite of the finding of the board to carry on its operations to the detriment to the public? In that regard and in that way this legislation makes of some real service the past legislation which has been enacted by this parliament on the subject of combines. I have only mentioned certain of the remedies which may be introduced, but I think the hon. member cannot attach too much importance in cases of this kind to the effect which publicity will have. In that connection I am inclined to think that much good will come of this legislation. Parties will know when they are entering into a combine in restraint of trade that their operations may be investigated and they will be careful, and in that way the public having the means of getting at the facts of the case will be insured against harmful action on the part of these particular combinations. We have the experience of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act as a case in point. There we have had something like 80 applications, and I think in 74 cases of the 80, as the result of inquiry, as the result of bringing to light different facts in regard to industrial disputes, the parties have thought it unwise to carry on the fight. They have thought it much better to make a settlement and an adjustment of their difficulties, public opinion having made its influence felt, than to defy public opinion by going against the decision of a board. The same thing will haoDen under these investigations. The combines will be investigated, if investigation reveals an undesirable situation, the members of the combines will very soon see in what position they are going to be placed before the -public unless they change their tactics, and the chances are that in many cases during the course of the investigation itself, a combine will see its way clear to

mend its ways, and the board will be able to tell the public that while such and such a thing was going on before the investigation, during the investigation the parties had mended their ways. That was exactly the case when the select committee appointed by this House in 1888, of which the late Mr. Clarke Wallace was chairman, was conducting an inquiry. A number of the combines were brought before the committee and during the course of the inquiry itself some of them changed their tactics. Now if that was the case under that machinery, there is every reason why it should be the case under the machinery provided by this Act.
I went pretty fully into these features on the second reading, but I may emphasize this further point seeing that the hon. member from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) raised the question as to who should pay the expenses in the event of long prosecutions. Under this measure the government will assume the expenses of the investigation and therefore the' position of parties seeking redress is very materially changed. The member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) asked a question in regard to the cement merger, and said the Minister of Finance had promised to see during the session that a Bill was brought in to meet the case of the cement merger. It is not my wish to say whether or not the cement merger has enhanced prices unduly. I do not think any one would be justified in making a statement of that kind without having the facts before him. What is the position to-day under the legislation we have? If any one wishes to proceed against the cement merger or a group of consumers wish to proceed against the cement merger, they have to bring a criminal action or they have to make representations to the government sufficiently strong to induce he government to start a judicial inquiry, and they have to be prepared to pay the cost of that inquiry themselves. There are many consumers in this country who will hesitate to ask for an investigation on those conditions. They would hesitate to put the men who are associated with the cement merger in the position of defendants in a criminal action and they would hesitate to render themselves liable to the costs which might be involved in a long judicial inquiry. Under this measure which has been brought down to the House any six persons may go before a judge of a high court, any six of my hon. friend's constituents who feel that they are being unfairly dealt with by this cement merger, may lay before the judge the evidence which they have, the kind of evidence which he has read to the House this morning, and submit to the judge that there is a prima facie case. All they are obliged to do is to swear to the effect that they believe these statements to be true, that as
consumers the cement merger has operated to their detriment, and that they believe it is in the public interest that an investigation should be made into this merger. If they persuade the judge that a case exists for investigation, the judge issues an order for an investigation. Thereupon the six consumers who have made the complaint are asked to name a member of the board to inquire into the business of the cement merger, and the cement merger in turn are asked to name their member of the board, the two to agree upon the chairman. These three gentlemen appointed in this way have all the powers of a court. They have power to send for the books of the company, they have power to compel the production of documents, and to examine under oath and to take evidencs and having gone fully into the whole question they prepare a report which they give to the public on the results of their investigation.
Who is charged with the. responsibility of hunting up evidence and presenting it to that board, these six men?

After the judge states that in his opinion a prima facie case has been made out, that it is in the public interest that an investigation should take place, then the six men are relieved of further responsibility. The onus is not upon them, it has become a case of investigating in the public interest by the public itself. The measure provides that the government may appoint counsel to gather evidence and present it to the board and the fees of that counsel are to be met by the government The different members of the board are free to ask any question and to send for any document. They are an investigating board assisted by counsel, their expenses and his are paid by the government. In that way a thorough examination will be carried out.
Does the government bear all the expenses in connection with these investigations on both sides?

The government, of course, has to put some limit to the expense. If the parties wish to bring in an array of attorneys and are not satisfied with the counsel which the government has appointed, if they desire to have half a dozen counsel of their own, that is their lookout,' and they may have to meet that part of the expense. But the expense which is neees-sary in the public interest will be borne by the government. The government is prepared to meet all that in its opinion is necessary to get at the facts of the case thoroughly and accurately. Now to conclude the reference to this merger, many of the gentlemen who are associated with the cement merger claim that they are being put in a false light before the public, and

that, as a matter of fact the cement business has been carried on in Canada in the past in such a way that the business has been almost ruined, and that all the merger has done has been to place the different concerns that are in it in a position where through their co-operation they are enabled to get a reasonable and fair profit. If such is the case, it will be brought out on examination, and a finding of that sort made by the board would satisfy the public mind that it had been mistaken as to the cement merger, and that, as a matter of fact, the merger, instead of holding up the public, was doing what it was in the interests of a large industry in this country to do.
Would the board have power to take into consideration the overcapitalization of a merger such as this, because no doubt two-thirds of it is water.

Certainly, that is just what the investigation is for. You have a board appointed with all the powers of a court, and the members of that board can put any question they wish to the company that is being investigated, and undoubtedly the question of over-capitalization would be one of the first to be investigated. If the board after carefully going into the evidence found that the cement merger was only making a reasonable profit
Profit on what?

On capital invested. A reasonable profit, I assume, is the profit on the money put into the business. If the board found that, as respects the cement merger there was only a reasonable profit on capital invested, and if the evidence substantiated it, then the cement merger would be in a stronger position before the public than they could ever hope to be otherwise, in view of the suspicion and distrust that for some reason or other has arisen. On the other hand, if the board should report that the investigation showed that the cement merger had taken advantage of the situation, the government has power under this legislation, without going any further, to lower the duties on cement. If the board reported that in their opinion the cement company ought to reduce the price, and the cement company persisted in not doing so, then a criminal proceeding might be taken and the parties instituting the proceedings would have before them the benefit of the evidence brought out at the investigation. I think it will be admitted there is no concern in this country that can afford to defy public opinion. If you get public opinion intelligently shaped and have it properly focused on an-industrial evil, then it is not likely that those responsible will continue that evil in the teeth of public opinion. It is in this belief Mr. KING.
that it is hoped this measure may accomplish its object.

Do I understand that the aggrieved persons will have to lodge information themselves before anything is done, and that the minister will not take the initiative? The minister stated that those connected with the cement business urged that they were only receiving a fair price for cement now. Well, last year we bought cement at $1.80 per barrel, and the large cement company situated within sight of these buildings was able to pay 10 per cent on the basis of that price. Surely when the cement costs 60 cents a barrel more this year there is reason for legitimate complaint on the part of consumers.
The minister has talked so much that I do not know whether he has answered my question or not. What I want to know simply is: who is going to pay these six men at the outset.

If the six men prove to the judge that they have made out their case, the judge may award such disbursements as he thinks necessary, and the government has power to pay these disbursements, it appearing that these men have acted in the public interest. On the other hand, if six persons come along with a complaint which is frivolous or which is made for some mischievous reason, and are unable to make out a case before the judge, then they must look to paying the costs themselves. I think that is reasonable.

They told us there was no combine so far as they were concerned, that a large percentage of the cbment business was not in the merger, that there was actual bona fide competition between the merger and the outside companies, and that they felt sure the public would get the cement at a reasonable and fair price. ing these contentions, but in view of what the hon. member for Selkirk has said, I think it only fair that I should present to the House the contentions of that deputation.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a few remarks on this question, the county which I have the honour to represent being highly interested in _ all that pertains to the subject under discussion. I find that about ten years ago a powerful company called the American Tobacco Company began its operations in the province of Quebec. Later on they assigned all their rights to another very powerful company, the Imperial Tobacco Company. They bought all the tobacco factories established in the counties of Joliette, Montcalm and L'Assomption, to the great prejudice of the farmers interested in the growing of tobacco. These companies stipulated that the vendors would be precluded, during the space of twenty years, from engaging in the manufacture of tobacco and from having any interest whatsoever in that industry, thus inserting a clause which was utterly prohibitory.
The law which permits the prohibitory clause, as between sellers and buyers, requires three conditions; 1st, that the object should be fullv determined; 2nd. that the place should be accurately specified, and 3rd, that the duration of the contract should be determined. In the case of the companies who bought the factories of the counties in question, they stipulated, in
order to evade the law, that the vendor would have the right to engage in that industry in Alaska or on the banks of the Yukon river. Such a clause clearly indicates that the object in view was simply to evade the law. Indeed, had not this exception been made, the contract would have been radically null and void. But in order to escape the law, it was specified that the vendor would have the right to engage in the manufacture of tobacco in what is known as the Yukon district.
The people who thus sold their manufactures obtained rather high prices from that company who own millions. These sales have caused great damages to the farmers by drawing away from these counties quite a number of factories. Moreover, the Imperial Tobacco Company, being the only buyers of the tobacco crop, controlled the prices and gave the farmers just what they pleased to give them. As a matter of fact, the company regulates the prices and the conditions which they see fit to impose on the producers.
I desire to know from the hon. Minister of Labour whether this Bill can reach such contracts as these. I see by sections 22 and 23 of the present Bill that whoever shall buy out, or prevent competition, or even shall unduly restrict the manufacture or production of any commercial commodity, shall be liable to rather a heavy fine or even to imprisonment.
This is all very well, but there is one point on which I desire to be informed by the minister. I desire to know whether this law shall be retroactive in its effects, or in other words, whether it shall apply to those who have in the past bought these factories with the restrictions which I have pointed out. Because my constituency is very much interested in being able to obtain the power to reopen the factories which have been closed after having been bought by the powerful corporation, ' The Imperial Tobacco Company.'
In my opinion this law is very important from the standpoint of those who are engaged in agricultural pursuits, and especially in the growing of tobacco like the people of the county of Montcalm.
If it is possible to annul or at least to modify the existing contracts; if it is possible to bring before the Board of Control mentioned in this Bill such cases as these, so that the people who sold opt their establishment could reopen their old manufactures, the hon. minister shall deserve the heartfelt gratitude of that part of the country where people are engaged in the tobacco industry, and in particular of that part of the country which I have the honour to represent in this House.
It is my desire that the minister should tell me whether this law will effect that kind of existing contracts.

I am quite prepared to give this new measure a trial, and especially to give it consideration in view of the introduction of the principle of publicity in these matters. But I also wish to say that the Bill commends itself to me because this government has accepted a principle that I fought for for many years in this House, namely, that the government, when it introduces a Bill to remedy a grievance, ought to provide machinery under the Bill for the enforcement of the law. Hitherto that has been neglected. I was laughed out of the House almost at that time by the Minister of Justice, who said that he was the Attorney General for the Dominion, as he called himself, that he was responsible for the enforcement of Dominion Acts, and that the Attorney Generals of the provinces were also responsible for the enforcement of them. But now I see there is provision in this Act for its enforcement, that the Minister of Justice can institute actions, can retain counsel, that the Governor in Council will also act, and that the patent law can be enforced in this respect. This is great progress compared with what we had in the past. It is a change and it is just an other of the things which I have pressed upon this House and which received little consideration at the start, but which are now recognized and are being adopted as general principles.
They are all the time doing it.	.

My hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) says they are all the time doing it. But this is not an omnibus Act to cure the grievances in connection * with other general Acts. For instance, if there is something wrong in connection with patents and patent laws, the effective remedy is in the Patent Act, and I believe the Patent Act ought to be greatly.enlarged and extended on the lines of the German and British Patent Acts in order to afford protection to the people. We ought to have a system in this country that would automatically bring about the cancellation of a patent if the patent was being used to the detriment of the public or for the unfair enhancement of prices. If mergers are possible, as they now are, and if they are grievances, automatically, the law that controls the capitalization of the merger ought to in some way intervene and compel a reduction in the capitalization. We have no control of capitalization to-day, and a great many of the economic evils of the country are due to unfair capitalization. Also, in the matter of the tariff, if there is a grievance, in consequence of unfair treatment and the enhancement of prices, the tariff itself ought to automatically operate so as to bring the grievance to a finish. I think this principle should be more and more adopted of the federal government making appropriations, employing counsel, paying witnesses and doing all those things in order to enforce its own laws. It does not do to leave the administration of the large federal Acts to the provinces, or to leave to them the expense of enforcing these laws. It is true that the provinces do enforce the Criminal Code, but there are grave breaches of the Criminal Code in this country that you cannot have enforced by provincial action, and more and more the principle recognized in this Bill should be extended to all the great federal Acts. We have another instance of the extension of this principle in the Railway Act, but, certainly under the Railway Act, you ought to have a general prosecuting attorney in the public interest representing the Crown and the public, and whose duty it would be to see that the Act was enforced. The merit of this and all those remedial Bills that are being passed in this country to deal with public grievances and correct abuses, de- ; pends upon the federal government spending its money freely and employing Crown officers to enforce the law. That will be ] the future of it and of all those Acts of a [DOT] remedial character that we have passed in the last few years. Certainly it is a matter < of satisfaction to me to know that while i the proposition that I made in this House some years ago that this government ! should be responsible for the enforcement ) of its own Acts was ridiculed, it has at : last been recognized, and there is a fair i Mr. HENDERSON.
hope that the principle being accepted with respect to this particular Act will be embodied in a great many others.

We have heard from hon. gentlemen in this House about the cement merger, and we have heard from other. hon. gentlemen about the rubber merger. It would almost seem that every member of the House has a special merger that he knows something about. We have had in the city of Quebec lately what is known as the Quebec merger. The 'Canadian Electric Company, the Canadian Gas Company, the Frontenac Gas Company, and the Quebec Railway, Light and Power Company have all combined, and from the very minute they did combine the people of Quebec found the price of gas went up from $1 per 1,000 cubic feet to $1.50 per 1,000 cubic feet. It is a curious coincidence that the moment these companies combine the citizens should find that the price of gas goes up. The port of Quebec has a grievance in regard to the freight rates that are charged to that port, and I have here a letter from one of our leading merchants in Quebec in which he says that the North Atlantic West Bound Freight Conference lines is practically a combine, which includes the Allan Line, the_ Dominion Line, the Canadian Pacific Railway Line, the Manchester Liners, and Donaldson Brothers. This West Bound Freight Conference line has put in rates to Quebec

And when we consider that the port of Quebec is 180 miles nearer to European ports than is the port of Montreal, one can hardly find a reason why they make such discriminatory rates to the detriment of the city of Quebec. Perhaps the minister would give us an explanation of the Bill, particularly informing us whether it differs, and if so in what respect, from the Bill which was before the House two sessions ago.

If I am rightly informed, this Bill was before the Senate two years ago. There were some objections to it, and it was considered to be of such importance that there was an investigation held and evidence taken before a special committee for the purpose of ascertaining what remedy needed to be applied. Last year the Bill was again before the Senate and was passed by that House, and sent over to the House of Commons; but it was in the dying hours of the session, and did not go through. This year the Bill came again before the Senate. As it_ is now before the House, it contains certain amendments which were made by the special Committee on Marine and Fisheries, after an investigation in winch evidence was taken. The object of the Bill is to restrict the contracting power of a ship-owner, whenever in his bill of lading or other document he inserts any clause to relieve himself from responsibility for loss or damage, whether as a result of his own negligence or want of care or not.
I understand that complaints were made by shippers that in bills of lading there were provisions of this kind so th^t when goods were damaged or lost, the loss was sustained by them instead of by the shipowner, and the object is to prevent him relieving himself of responsibility in this way.
On section 4, certain clauses prohibited in bill of lading.
I did not catch what the Solicitor General said as to the similarity of this Bill to the one passed by the Senate.
It is practically the same Bill.
Perhaps the minister would let us know when there is any change in any section of the Bill.

I understand that clause 10 has been added as a new section. It was not in the old Bill as presented to the Senate, and it has been added as the result of the investigation held before the Marine and Fisheries Committee. Complaints were made that certain numbers of pieces of wood were shipped and that w..en they got across the ocean, measurements were taken, and if the measurements and standards did not tally with the measurements and tallies of the shippers,

the loss was on the ship-owners. That ha.s been changed. so that when the shipowner delivers the exact number of pieces < he has received, he will be relieved from liability whether the measurements or standards agree or not. That is the only change I understand that has been made in the Act.
On section 6,

These words ' or from latent defect ' were added by the committee on Marine and Fisheries at the instance of William Thompson and Company, of St. John, who said it would be a hardship sometimes if there was some latent defect in a ship such as a defective boiler which could not possibly be found out, and the ship went to sea with a very valuable cargo and was lost by reason of that latent defect, that the ship-owners should be held liable. That has always been the law, and these words do not change it.
Is it not going a long way to say that a ship-owner should not be held responsible for a latent defect. No one could inspect the ship but himself.
It only applies to cases where it is impossible to discover a latent defect. There are many cases in which it. is not possible for a ship-owner to know.

That is hardly the amendment. If there is a latent defect, I do not like the idea of the responsibility being put upon anybody but the person who has control of the inspection and who has the power to order all such defects to be corrected. I do not like it to be put upon any one but the owner of the ship who should be able to discover the defect.

If the hon. minister will look at the section he will see that it reads ' If the owner of any ship transporting merchandise ot property from any port in Canada exercises due diligence to make the ship in all respects sea-worthy and properly manned,' The ship owner is bound by this to exercise due diligence, and he is also bound under the shipping Act to have his ship inspected every year, and to have a certificate carried by the captain that his ship has undergone proper inspection. If he has exercised due diligence, and there is a latent defect he has the right to be relieved from liability.

I do not disagree with what the hon. member says, but I am afraid the Act itself would not have quite the effect that his argument implies. ' If the owner of any ship exercises due diligence to make the ship in all respects seaworthy and properly manned '-
And equipped.

That is all Tight as the section is printed, so far as it
goes, but if there was a latent defect in a shiD then the owner could say, I used due diligence to make the ship seaworthy and properly manned and equipped, and I am not liable for the latent defects. He could discover these latent defects by proper inspection.

Section 6, it seems to me goes very far. It seems to exempt altogether the owners of the boat from liability for damage caused by negligence or want of proper skill on the part of the servants or agents of the ship-owner. That certainly is contrary to most rules of legal liability. The master is entrusted with the employment of the servants, he has entirely to do with the employment of servants, and when we say that the servant of the master may do as he pleases, and if his action results in damage to the owner of the cargo the master is not responsible, we are going very far. It is not so in the case of railway accidents. If the engineer or brakeman is guilty of negligence the company is liable, and it seems to me dangerous to say that the owner of a vessel shall escape scott free if his employees are guilty of negligence in the management or navigation of the ship. They may run into another boat or a dock or a rock, but no matter how negligent those in charge may be no person is responsible for the loss of the cargo in the ship. I am not very familiar with these marine matters, but it seems to me a dangerous thing to place the owner of the cargo entirely at the mercy of any employee of the ship if the owner of the ship is not to be responsible.

As I understand the common law has always been that the owner employs the best master he can get, a man in whom he has confidence, and if this man, by improper navigation or by not doing what he should do, destroys the ship, the owner is not liable for the damage to the cargo. It would be unreasonable to make him liable. The running of a ship is very hazardous, it is not at all on the same basis as the operation of a railway. A railway company gets certain franchises from the country, it. has certain rights which it gets from the public. A ship gets nothing whatever from the public. The owner of the ship embarks his capital in a hazardous business, and it would be unreasonable to hold him liable for loss on the cargo under such circumstances. He is just as anxious to save his ship, and get it safely to port as is the owner of the cargo that his goods shall get to port, unless he is a scoundrel anxious to lose his ship for the sake of the insurance.
Is not the owner of a ship a common carrier?

No and yes. It has never been held in the courts that he has the same liability as the owner of a railway or a common carrier on land. The owner of the ship does not earn his freight unless he lands his goods on the other "side, and consequently you can depend on him to get the goods there. Suppose he does not know what the goods are worth. It often turns out that goods are worth a great deal of money, and the freights are very low. A man may be carrying freignt at a few dollars a ton that is worth millions, and it would be unreasonable to hold him responsible on account of the small freight he gets if anything should happen the cargo through carelessness, &c.
I thought they had to put the value on the bill of lading.

Not at all. There is often no value stated in the bill of lading. It discloses the number of tons, and of course the freight, but not the value of the goods. This Bill goes_ a long distance towards taking away the rights the ship-owner now has. Under the present common law he has the right to make a contract, but you are depriving him of that right which nearly every person enjoys under the law. We deprive him of the right to contract with the owner of the goods in regard to the care of the goods. There are some cases where it is quite proper that the owner of a ship should be allowed to make a contract to relieve himself of liability, and where the owner of the goods would be quite willing to accept the liability in order to get the owner of the ship to carry his goods. This, then, is a compromise to which the shipowners of Montreal, and other parts of Canada have agreed. The whole question was threshed out before the 'Senate Committee, and later on before a committee of this House. At that committee the following shipping lines were represented: The Allan line, the Quebec Steamship line, the Llder-Dempster line, the McLean-Kennedy line, the Hamburg American line, the Dominion Coal Company, the Donaldson line, and the Thompson line. The Dominion Millers were also represented by men who well understood the business they were dealing with, and gave it a good deal of attention. The Manufacturers' Association was represented, and a number of other interests. ^ The Bill was carefully threshed out, and if we undertake to change it without very careful thought we may be creating a condition of affairs that will cause great disturbance in the commerce of Canada. The Bill goes a great distance in protecting the owners of the goods.. That, of course, is its intention. It arose through the conditions that were being inserted in
Mr. SINCLAIR,
the bills of lading granted by the steamship people in Montreal. In that form of bill of lading they inserted clauses relieving the steamship of the liability which should really have been assumed by the steamship, such liability as putting the goods in contact with other goods that would damage them. The right was also put in the bill of lading to deliver the goods to the consignee notwithstanding the fact that the bill of lading had ben endorsed to a bank. There were in fact certain clauses in the bills ^ of lading in common use among the shipping people on the St. Lawrence that should not have been there, and that is what gave rise to the Bill -in the first place. ^ Many concession were made by the shipping people, these concessions were accepted by the representatives of the Manufacturers Association, and the Millers, and I trust the members will understand that the words of this Bill have not been placed here without a great deal of thought and care. The House ought to accept the Bill unless they can point out something very improper in the language.

The shipper of goods can protect himself by insuring his cargo. That is the whole point at issue. When you ship a cargo you insure it for its full value, sometimes for a little more than its value on account of fluctuations in price.

Mr. Chairman, the shipper can insure for the full value of his goods, but to cover the case of the old bill of lading we would require to insure under the all-risks clause, which covers every kind of damage. It costs a great deal more to insure under that clause than under the ordinary clause. However, this section, in my mind, would reduce the cost of insurance to the shipper as it would enable him to insure under the ordinary clause. The trouble in the past has been that the through bill of lading received by the shippers in Canada did not hold the vessel owners liable in any way whatever. It did not even oblige them to deliver the same goods that you shipped; it held them liable to deliver the same kind of goods, but not the same goods. Then it permitted them to deliver the goods to the party to whom they were shipped before the original bill of lading was delivered up. This was the principle object in asking for the new through bill of lading now. Formerly we who shipped from inland points did not really know what our Shipping Bill contained. We took a bill of lading from the railway com-oany, which held the railway company liable for any damage, and that simply stated that we came under the Ship's hill when they handed over the goods to the steamship company. Now, what is needed is a Bill that will hold the steamship

company liable for the goods. However, as my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has stated, this Bill is in the nature of a compromise between the shippers and the ship owners, and it would be in the interest of the shippers to let the Bill pass as it is, because if any amendments were made to it they would b-lock the Bill for this year and the shippers would have no protection durins the coming year. This Bill will afford a degree of protection to them, and therefore it would be better to let it go through as it is.

The provisions of the Bill which restrict the liberty of a shipowner by means of stipulations in the bill of lading relieving himself from responsibility, are a great advantage to the shipper, and to that extent the Bill is an advantage to the shipper. But I think we require to proceed with care when it is proposed, because those particular sections give certain advantages to the shipper to impose upon him a disadvantage by other sections of the Bill. There may be a sufficient reason for enacting this section, but it certainly is a section which relieves the ship-owner, that is, the ship-owner who is engaged in transporting goods, from responsibilities which undoubtedly were incumbent upon him at common law. I was surprised to hear the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sinclair) say that a ship-owner was not a carrier and did not come under the common law regarding carriers. I think he is a carrier in precisely the same sense as a railway company, if he carries on the business of a carrier, that is, if he transports goods in a ship. The mere fact that a man owns a vessel does not make him a carrier, but if he uses it to carry goods, he becomes a carrier the same as a railway company is a carrier. A railway company, because it owns a railway, is not thereby a common carrier, hut when it engages in the business of carrying, then it comes under the common law regulating carriers. Railway companies have special legislation affecting them, and this is special legislation made for the ship-owners. But when the hon. gentleman said that there never was any liability, that it never was the law that the shipowner engaged in the business of carrying goods was responsible for the loss that occurred by error in the management of the vessel, I must say he enunciated a proposition quite new to me. It is in fact because the ship-owner is a common carrier at common law, and as such would' he responsible to deliver the goods that he undertook to carry, and could excuse himself for their loss only on the ground that the loss was attributable either to the act of God or to the King's enemies, that there is any object- in making a section of this kind. It is clearly a section to modify the 254
responsibility which at common law lies upon the ship-owner as a common carrier. It seems to me to go exceedingly far, it is going to put the ship-owner in a different position, not only from that of common carrier, but it is going to put him in a different position as regards responsibility, from that occupied by every other person who employs others to act as his servants. The general rule of law is, that I am responsible for damage that is caused by the fault or negligence of my servant in the performance of the duty for which I employ him. Now, this is a provision that the ship-owner shall not be responsible for .damage caused b,y the fault of the servant in the performance of the duties for which he employs him, and its practical effect is that the ship-owner, even though he employed an incompetent captain, will not be responsible for the damage resulting from the incompetence of that captain in the management of the ship. It is true, it is required, as a condtion of this exemption, that he should exercise due diligence to make the ship in all respects seaworthy and properly to man it, so it will be on him to show the due diligence. But I think the effect of the section is to create an exceptional position for the ship-owner, it places him in a category by himself.
What does the hon. gentleman find in this proposed statute that enables the ship-owner to employ an incompetent captain and send him out with the ship?

I pointed out that of course he would have to establish that he had used diligence, but even though he may have used diligence, the captain that he has employed may prove to be incompetent, and still he is being relieved from damage resulting from mismanagement. Now we find here the words: 'error in navigation or mismanagement of the ship '. Those are errors attributable to the captain or officers of the vessel, and the fact that they make such errors would at all events, in relation to that particular error, show them to be incompetent, -and yet we relieve the ship-owner from responsibility. I will not discuss whether the general rule of the law is a good rule, but I certainly think that it cannot be disputed that the general rule of law is that I am responsible for damage that is done by my employee if that damage is caused by him while he is in the performance of the duties for which I employ him; and if you pass this section you place the ship-owner in a lifferent position from any other employer, and you relieve him from responsibility for the incompetency of the people whom he employs. That is clearly a most material liminution of the responsibility of the shipowner at common law as a carrier, and as an employer of persons. Whether the ad-



vantages to the shipper from the other sections of the Act are sufficiently great to compensate for the disadvantages, would perhaps be a matter of question. I think myself that this House ought not to adopt this legislation on the supposition that it never was the law that the ship-owner was responsible for mismanagement of the vessel by his employees.

There can be no doubt that at common law the principle laid down by the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) is correct. 1 My hon. friend will agree that when parties have contracted, however, in regard to the carriage of goods, this clause always appears in a bill of lading for the protection of the shipper. And what are we doing here in this Bill? It might be said in a way tha.t we are making a bill of lading to govern the shipment of goods from Canada and into Canada. We are following in that respect the example which was set by the United States when they adopted some years ago what is known as the Harter Act, and the clauses which are incorporated here are a reproduction of that legislation which was settled at the suggestion of the commercial world in the United States. In declaring what shall be in the bill of lading it might be said that we are declaring what shall be the bill of lading for the future. We are not doing anything that is unfair to either party. The various interests that appeared before the committee on this subject were representative of the shippers and the carriers, the latter of whom were anxious to have a definite and clear bill of lading made a matter of law. While under the common law these liabilities did exist on the shipowner, as a matter of fact they did not exist on account of being contracted against, and I do not think there is anything anomalous in reproducing in the law what is practically in every bill of lading in the coun-* try. The fact that the different interests watched with the greatest keenness in order to see that no undue advantage was given to either side is the best evidence that the measure is a well considered one.

I am afraid my hon. friend from St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) misunderstood what I intended to convey.' Under the law, ias at present, the ship-owner is allowed to make a contract, and in every charter party and bill of lading he is very caTeful to contract himself out of as much liability as he can. For hundreds of years, in every one of these shipping contracts it has always been the custom of ship-owners to contract themselves out of the specific things that are mentioned in section 7, such as: loss arising from Are, dangers of the sea, the acts of God and the King's enemies, and inherent vice of the thing carried. These are among the things that Mr. DOHERTY. '
have appeared in every bill of lading and charter party that has been in existence in British countries for very many years. We are now by this Act taking away from the ship-owner the right to make a contract that will contract himself out of liability, but we think this clause is a reasonable one.

The shipper is obliged now to sign the bill of lading presented to him ot otherwise he cannot ship his goods. If a loss should be sustained through the negligence of the common carrier and in common law he weTe sued for damages, would not the court determine which of these provisions in the contract were reasonable and which unreasonable, and only allow to prevail those which were reasonable?

I think the courts have always held a man liable foT the consequence of his own negligence. He can contract himself out of his negligence, and if the owner of the goods agrees to that contract.you have a contract between the two. but that is the thing we are trying to avoid. The committee arrived at the conclusion that the provisions in clause 7 were reasonable. That is the meaning of it and nothing more.
On section 7,

There is something in this section to which I would call the special attention of the committee, because it involves so serious an error that I doubt very much if it could have been intended that the section should be couched in these precise words. At all events I do not think it could have been intended to produce the effect which the enactment of the clause would produce. I quite agree that it would be a proper thing to exempt the shipowner from loss arising from the different causes whioh are mentioned in this section, provided such loss arises without his fault or privity or the fault ot privity of his servants, for whom he is responsible. But, as I read the section as drawn, it exempts the ship-owner from responsibility if the damage is the result of any one of the causes enumerated there, without considering at all whether that cause is attributable to his fault or the fault of those for whom he is responsible. For instance, under the section as drafted, the ship-owner would have nothing to do but say your goods were destroyed by Are, and then he would be exempt under the section. I submit he should be called upon to show that the goods were destroyed by Are which was not attributable to his fault or to the fault of those for whom he was responsible.

Under section 4, he cannot contract himself out of liability for negligence.
