Yes, but in this section it is not a question of contracting himself out of anything; the law itself here says, that the ship-owner shall have no responsibility, regardless of what contract he may make, for the lo-ss of goods destroyed by fire. It may be that the shipper is insured against that loss, but I have difficulty in convincing myself that it was intended to say, as this section says, that the shipowner in order to be relieved, need only prove that the cause was fire. Fire is not a thing that necessarily excludes the idea of fault on the part of persons in charge of the place where the fire occurred, on the contrary, probably in the majority of cases, fire is due to somebody's fault. When you merely prove that the goods were burnt, the question remains absolutely undetermined in any way whether that is a loss attributable to the fault of the ship-owner or his employees. In dealing with a section of this kind, which has nothing to do with what a man may -contra ot himself out of, but which is fixing the legal liability, you want to remember in making statutory provisions what the position o'f the party was in the absence of these provisions. His position in the absence of any provision to relieve him, was that his obligation was to produce the goods or explain why he did not, and to so explain it as to exclude the idea that it was his fault that he did not produce them. The only excuses the common law recognizes were the act of God and the King's enemies. I am not -arguing that a man should not be exempt from responsibility for the causes enumerated in this section; what I -contend for is that he should be_ so relieved from -that liability, only provided that the happening of anv one of these things mentioned is not aftri-butable to bis fault. I know it may bo answered that as regards some of the things enumerated in this section thev could not be his fault, such as the act of God or the King's enemies or inherent vice m the things carried. Mr. SINCLAIR. That is not his fault. Mr. DOHERTY. Certainly not, but the answer to that is that the common law relieves him from that liability. That clearly could not be a cause of liability because that could not be his fault. The act of God, or the King's enemies or a defect in the goods that were furnished to him would not be his fault, and the common law would relieve him of all liability, but when you come to fire it might bo hi? fault. Mr. SINCLAIR. Fire is the only one that might be his fault. Mr. DOHERTA. I beg your pardon. When you come to the perils of the sea it is quite true that the peril is not his 2541	fault, but an accident resulting from it might be his fault if he has not taken proper precautions to avoid it. Under the the very same sort of legislation you will find judgments of the court to the effect that, though the immediate cause is the peril of the -sea, the ship-owner is responsible for the accident by which his vessel succumbed to the peril of the sea in that, for instance, the vessel was not seaworthy or, until we had the immediately preceding section, that she was not properly managed. With those exceptions, the act of God, the King's enemies and defects in the goods themselves, all of which would exempt him at common law', I submit that the law should be made to read that the ship-owner shall not be held liable for loss arising without his fault or the fault or privity ^ of any person from whom he is responsible from the causes mentioned in that section. I think that t-he explanation of _ how the section comes to be worded in this way is to be found in the fact that the people who drew it followed the example of the revisers of the statutes in 1906 and who, with all respect, I think, have made a very serious error. In 1906 they purported to revise chapter 82 of the _ Revised Statutes of 1886 and, more particularly they revised section 2 of that statute. In what purported to be a reproduction of section 2 they entirely altered the sense of section 2 apparently because they thought there would be an advantage in dividing the paragraphs of the section and giving each one a number. Section 2 of chapter 82, Revised Statutes, 1886, dealt with this subject precisely in the way that I contend it should be dealt with now and its provision reads as follows. After declaring the liabilitv for the loss of or damage to goods entrusted to them for conveyance they went on to say, in subsection 4, section 2: Provided, that they shall not he liable to any extent whatsoever to make good any loss or damage happening without their actual fault or privity, or the fault or neglect of their agents, servants or employees,- (a)	To any goods on board any such vessel, or delivered to them for conveyance therein, by reason of fire or the dangers of navigation. Exempting there substantially the very two causes mentioned here, but making it an additional requirement that the accident should happen without the fault of the ship-owner or carrier or the persons for whom he is responsible. Then they went on: (b)	Arising from any defect in or from the nature of the goods themselves, or from armed robbery or other irresistible force. Then they went on with other provisions I am not quite clear whether they are the same here or not. When the revision took place in 1906, and when the re-

visers came to reproduce that section, they made it read:
Carriers by water shall be liable for the loss of or damage to goods entrusted to them for conveyance, except that they shall hot be liable when such loss or damage happens,-
(a)	without their actual fault or privity, or without the fault or neglect of their agents, servants or employees; or,
(b)	by reason of fire or the dangers of navigation.
So that they did what this Bill is now doing; they made the absence of fault one distinct cause of exemption from liability, and then they made fire and the perils of navigation and these other things that are enumerated other causes of exemption from liability, producing practically . the result that even though the fire should be attributable to the fault of the ship-owner, nevertheless, it was to be ,a cause of exemption from liability. As I said in the beginning, I cannot convince myself that that was intended, for they enact that without regard to the question whether you are in fault or not, you shall not be responsible provided the damage be due to fire, and yet what the section says is clear from the fact that they make the absence of fault one distinct and substantial ground of relief from liability standing by itself. Then they go on to make fire and all the other things separate and distinct grounds of relief from liability. I do not know how this Bill was drafted, but it seems to me that it is the result of following the bad example of the gentlemen who drafted the Bevised Statutes in 1906, and who, in the Act as put in the revision of 1906, drifted away from what was the perfectly sound and correct .statement of what ought to be causes of exemption from liability, namely, fire and the perils of navigation, etc., provided the [DOT] loss was not attributable to the fault or occurred without the. fault of t'he ship-owner or the persons whom he employed. What I would suggest and what it seems to me would make it a perfectly reasonable law and not entail any injury upon the ship owner, is that in the second line of the section, after the word ' arising ' there be inserted the words ' without their actual fault or privity, or without the fault or neglect of their agents, servants or employees'. That would bring the wording back to the wording of the provision of section 2 of chapter 82, which was the provision intended to be merely reproduced from that section in the revision of the statutes of 1906, section 964, and which would set the law forth on what I submit would be a reasonable basis. Then it would go on ' or from,' etc.

Since recess I have had a talk with my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) and I have also Mr. DOHERTY.
taken occasion to consult some Englishspeaking gentlemen about the phraseology of the section. Here is a question of English grammar and phraseology which I frankly admit I am not competent to decide, but I am t-old that this last phrase of section 7 'or for loss arising without their actual fault or privity or without the fault or neglect of their agents, servants or employees' is not a separate and distinct reason why they should be relieved from liability, but is a qualifying phrase which ought to be read with the rest of the section and applied to the whole section. Then, if it is the act of God, or if the ship is burned, the 'Ship-owner shall not be liable provided there is no fault on the part of the master, servants or employees. I do Mot claim to be competent to judge when it comes to a question of English grammar. My hon. friend compares the statute of 1886 with the revised statute of 1906. The language of the Bill is exactly the language of the revised statute of 1906. I am not prepared to admit that the change in the language was made in the revision of the statute. There have been intervening amendments made to the .statute of 1886. There may have been a discussion in the House on those amendments justifying the amendment as it now stands in the revised statutes. That I am not prepared to say, because I had .not time during the recess to look over the statutes from 1886 to 1906 to see whether there had been any amendments between the consolidation and the revision. There mav have been, as the hon. member for St. Anne says, a slip on the part of those who revised the statutes. Before accepting the amendment suggested, I think we ought to find out whether the language of the statute of 1906 is not a repetition of the language used in statutes enacted subsequent to i886, and prior to 1906.

If the Solicitor General has been properly informed as to the last two lines governing the whole section, there can be no objection to the insertion of the words which the hon. member for St. Anne proposes, because in that case they will not add anything to the meaning of the section.
That is a question for you to decide.
I think it is rather a question for the law clerk to consider, and therefore, the hon. gentleman should allow that clause to stand.

I do not question that, it is precisely in 'section 964 where the error was made. I think the Solicitor General will find that there was no intervening legislation, and that section 964 of the revised statutes of 1906, merely purported to revise and reproduce the dispositions of subsection 4 and the following subsections of section 2 of chapter 82 of the Revised Statutes of 1886; but in the reproduction they made the proviso governing all the exemptions read, as the hon. gentleman has just read it, as a separate clause of exemption from liability. The hon, gentleman talks of the danger of a load of cotton being burned, and says that the ship-owner ought to be allowed to contract himself out of liability for it. I am not arguing against his being allowed to contract _ himself out of liability. The question is not with regard to contracting himself out of liability; it is with regard to determining what his legal liability is in the absence of a contract. The cargo of cotton may be an exceptional case. On the other hand, look at all the classes of goods which in themselves are not specially liable to fire. If a vessel burned and my goods burned in it, and the ship-owner-had not contracted on the subject at all, under this section all he would have to do would be to say that the goods were burned, and even though I proved that the fire was the result of the grossest fault on his part, he would go scot free, because fire per se, -without regard to what caused it, is made a ground of exemption. The hon. gentleman sa'-s that nobody would carry goods otherwise.
Not at the present rates of freight.

Up to 1906 people carried goods under the law which I am arguing for. I am not arguing that a
party shall not be free to contract himself out of liability, and he will naturally do that when he is dealing with goods that are particularly liable to fire. But in cases where there is no question of goods particularly liable to fire, where people* are shipping different kinds of goods in quantities, and the ship-owner does not deem it wise or desirable to stipulate that he shall not be liable for damage resulting from fire, if we are going to step in to his aid and relieve him of liability because it is a fire, even though it be proved that the fire is his direct fault, I must say that it is most dangerous legislation.
That might be possible, but not probable.

The law of the province of Quebec considers it so iprobaible that a fire, when it occurs, is attributable to the fault of the person at the place where it occurred or, to the fault of his employees, that in the case of landlord and tenant there is a presumption of the tenant's fault w7hen a building is destroyed by fire.
There was a case in which they held the contrary.

In that case it was held that the tenant might prove that it was not his fault. When the ship-owner to whom I give my goods, comes and saysc I do not deliver, there is m,y contract to deliver your goods, that is my contractual obligation, I do not deliver them. I say: Why don't you deliver, and he replies: Oh, they were burnt on my vessel, my vessel was burnt; I was in charge of it, and I have no further account to render to you. That is a hard enough situation for the shipper, but supposing I am in a position to go on and prove that that fire was the ship-owner's fault, nevertheless, under this legislation, I would have no recourse. Now, I submit that in the revision of the statute it was not intended to so alter the law. The hon. gentleman speaks of men in business refusing to be bound under the law in the sense which I contend for, yet I affirm without a moment's hesitation, that that certainly was the law up to 1906 when this revision of the statute took place, and still there was a good deal of shipping, and a good deal of business done. The hon. gentleman will find in the reports cases where precisely what I contend for was held, but under the exemptions as they stood prior to 1906, neither fire nor the perils of the sea were causes of relief from liability, unless it was shown that the fire was not attributable to the fault of the ship-owner or that as regards the perils of the sea the shipowner had properly guarded against those perils. Now7, I submit that while it is quite true that this section is carrying on

the law as it is expressed in the revision of 1906, it is materially altering the law as it stood up to that time, and altering it to create an exemption from liability in a case that I submit does not deserve sympathy at the hands of this parliament. After all, what is it that I am asking for in asking for the insertion of those words?
Is the liability as in the Revised Statutes of 1906 new, or has there been an,y intervening amendment to the statute of 1886?

My memory is that though the Revised Statute of 1906 purports to be a revision of chapter 82 of the revision of 1886, and refers to no other Act, I am under the impression, the very strong impression, that there was intervening legislation between 1886 and 1906, but in that intervening legislation the wording of 1886 [DOT]was retained. It is noteworthy that in the revised statutes each section refers back to the particular legislation which it purports to revise. I am fairly confident that I am making no mistake in what I have said, because it was not for the purpose of dealing with this Act that I had occasion to look into it. I had occasion to look into the legislation as it existed before the revision of 1906, and I distinctly remember my surprise to have it pointed out to me that the revision of 1906 altered the provision of the law. I am confident that whether there was intervening legislation between 1886 and 1906 or not, it is the revision of 1906 that first made this alteration. In that connection, I think it is noteworthy that the alteration, while a substantial alteration of the law, is effected merely by a rearrangement of the words. Where the law conies to be altered, it is done by taking a proviso covering all the subsections and making it a separate subsection. Now, I would be very much surprised if that is not merely the work of some gentleman occupying a more or less clerical position who thought he was making the thing look better by having each proviso with a number to it, with the result that he made that proviso a substantial disposition standing by itself. I am confirmed in that opinion, because I am convinced that the result is to produce a most unwarrantable condition of the law.

At the Marine apd Fisheries Committee at which this matter was brought up there were representatives of the Dominion Millers' Association, and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and I think every member of the committee who was present will give these gentlemen credit for doing everything they possibly could to put every liability on the shipowner, and take it off the shipper. But there was not one of these gentlemen who objected to the inclusion of fire in that Mr. DOHERTY.
section. They were quite content to include it after going over this whole business, and they were also the gentlemen who represented those associations before the Senate where this Bill was drafted, and afterwards passed, so that I think this matter has already received a great deal more attention than this House is in a position to give it, and with all due deference to every one I may say more intelligent thought and attention.
Hear, hear.

Because these gentlemen were present and had an opportunity of having the various matters argued before them, pro and con, on every clause that came up before them. Now the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) has given I have no doubt a very able legal argument in favour of the change he proposes, but at the same time he is a gentleman who lives on the land pretty much; he is acquainted with fire as it occurs in houses and places of that kind. So I take it that there are other reasons besides merely legal reasons which might have been brought out by the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) why this matter should remain as it is, because the word ' fire ' has been put in there after a great deal of consideration by those who were appearing for the ship-owners and also those who were appearing for the shippers. It has, as has already been mentioned, taken away from the shipowner the power to make his own contract with the shipper, something which has not been done by any nation having a large maritime fleet. It is not done by England, Italy, France, Germany or Norway and Sweden. These latter two countries are really stealing away a great deal of our own shipping business, especially as between the maritime provinces and the port [DOT]of Montreal. Is it the intention of those who are supporting the Bill to relieve the ship-owner absolutely from liability for negligence in these respects?

I understand that to be the intention. In cases where the damage arises from loss by fire or from damage of the sea or from the acts of God or public enemies, it was considered reasonable to relieve the ship-owner absolutely from responsibility for negligence, keeping in mind that the ship-owner has his own property in risk, that he has employed a captain competent under the law, that the ship is of value, that if the ship is lost the owner loses everything, and that he is also not in a position to insure the shipper's property. He can insure his own property but not yours.

Suppose the shipowner sets the fire or is contributary to it?
_ Does that relieve him from liability?
Oh, no, he would then be guilty of a crime.
You may send him to penitentiary for the crime of arson, but you are indicating there without any conditions that he shall be relieved from liability for loss by fire.
I do not understand it that way. It is the law now.

Of course under the common law the carrier is an absolute insurer, and has always relieved himself from liability by means of provisions in the bill of lading. I understand that this Bill is practically the result of a compromise between the two parties the shipowners and the shippers, and its provisions have been drafted after both parties have been heard and represented before the committee who had charge of the examination of the Bill before it came to the House.
Should parliament not exercise its judgment in enacting a law?

Certainly it is just to show the principles of the Bill. I understand as the leader of the opposition says, that it is relieving the owner of quite a responsibility, the responsibility for loss by fire, but on the other hand the nature of the case affords a certain guarantee. The idea of self-preservation is sufficiently well developed in every individual, whether at sea or on land, to stay his hand from performing any act that will lead to the destruction of his own life.

I realize the importance of that argument, but when actively engaged in the practice of my profession I had a good many of these maritime cases, and I am bound to say that the considerations which the hon. gentleman has mentioned have never tended very much to prevent acts of very great negligence at sea. I call to mind just one illustration. In the end it came down to a question of the direction of the wind, each ship insisting that having regard to the [DOT] direction of the wind, and the course she was steering the other should have given way. The result was that neither gave way and one went down. There was'no loss of life, but a very narrow escape.
I do not contend that the thing is impossible, I remarked that the chances, the probabilities, are very small.

How does the hon. gentleman explain the number of cases of fires that occur where it has been pleaded that the ship-owner was not responsible for fires. Then fires do not always destroy the whole vessel, only a portion of the goods may be destroyed. It must be remembered that we are dealing not only with

ocean going vessels, but with inland passenger boats as well.

My hon. friend in order to back his argument said that in 1886 the statute made it without fault or negligence on the part of the ship-owner, his agents or employees. But the ship-owner contracted himself out of liability not only in the case of fire, but of every possible eventuality, while loading. I was even told that when during the investigation before the committee it was found that they had inserted a clause whereby ship-owners carrying cheese and cattle contracted themselves out of any liability for manure or anything of that kind running through the deck, and damaging goods beneath. I suppose that this was a compensation for taking away from the ship-owner the right to contract himself out of liability. I am not a maritime man. If we are going to put this Bill through, I think that, ias my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) has said, it would be a disappointment to the parties most interested if we did not let it go as it is. The law will remain as it is in the revised statutes.

When I saw this discrepancy in the revised statutes I made a note of the necessity of amending the revised statutes. Now, I must confess that the thing is so palpably opposed to every sound principle, that I would feel rather ashamed to allow my amendment to stand The persons interested, whom the Solicitor General represents as having accepted this wording, were, I think, under the erroneous impression that the words as they . came at the end of the section qualified the whole section.

The hon. member fob Guysborough tells me not.
Mr. DOIIERT\. Well, to my mind to allow that to pass is creating a situation quite new, and giving a most exorbitant privilege to the ship-owner. You must remember that even with the words 'without fault or privity ' the ship-owner is going to escape if he can show that he did what he could to take care of his 3hip. Ihe hon. gentleman says: Of course they Will take care of their"ship; yes, and of course they will prove it every time. It is not asking much of a man to ask him to take care of his ship.	1
It is shifting the burden, of proof.

If he proves what the hon. gentleman says, that he always does, why, he will escape his liability. I think it is my duty at all events to submit my. amendment. I move:
That section 7 be amended by inserting in the second line after the word ' arising ' the words ' without their actual fault or privity or without the fault or neglect of their agents, servants or employees''; and by inserting in the ^tenth line thereof after the word ' arising ' the words ' from other cause.'

By placing these words in there ' without their actual fault or privity,' I ask the hon. gentleman how the ship-owner could be negligent in case of an act of God or of the King's enemies? I think he does not intend to make the amendment in the way he has made it, or to put it in the place he puts it, for it makes the whole section absurd. We have already enacted that the shipper is bound in all respects to see that his ship is seaworthy and properly equipped, and that section is binding upon us. The shipowner, therefore, cannot be liable for any negligence of his own, from dangers of the sea or other navigable water.

I have no objection to putting the words somewhere else. The absurdity of the section consists in our enacting a statutory legislation to say that the ship-owner shall not be liable for the loss resulting from the act of God or the King's enemies. That is the law now. It did seem to me, even if the words were put where they are, that everybody might take his chances that the courts would not interpret them to mean that after a man had proved that something was the act of God, he required to prove in addition that it was not his own fault.

If the hon. gentleman is acting in the interest of the owners of goods, he is taking a step that is very ]ikely to destroy the Bill altogether. There is no person who would be better pleased, if this Bill does not become law, than the ship-owner. This Bill is taking away valuable concessions and rights from the shipowning people of this country, and if the hon. gentleman pretends to be acting in the interest of the shipper and the people who own the goods, he will allow this section to pass as it stands.

I am not acting in the interest of anybody, either the ship-owner or the shipper-, I am trying to act as a member of this parliament to see that the legislation that goes through is in accordance with what I conceive to be justice. That is my entire motive in discussing this matter. The hon. gentleman, assuming that I represent the interests of the ship-

pers, says to me: Well, though this thing may be an unjust thing to you, if you do not consent to this unjust thing, -why, the ship-owners will refuse to allow this parliament to pass these other sections which this parliament considers are just, and which prevents them from contracting out of obligations which this parliament thinks should not be allowed to be contracted out of. I think it is putting this House in a humiliating situation that we should be told that we are to be compelled to do something prejudicial to one interest because if we do not, there is another interest that will force this House to refuse to pass three or four sections of this Act.
Supposing the hon. gentleman's amendment carries, what will be the effect on section 964 of the Canada Shipping Act?

This being the last legislation, it will repeal section 964 so far as there is a difference between them. But I am not quite clear that section 964 deals with precisely the same classes of carriers in all respects, but if it does, the effect of my amendment would be to modify section 964.

It is not clear. I might read the clause that I referred to for the hon. gentleman. It provides that they:
Shall not be liable when such loss or datnage happens by reason of fire or the dangers of navigation.

It will be modified to the extent of making it read, 'except that they shall not be liable when such loss or damage happens,' etc. The effect of my amendment, would be to strike out letter (a) simply, and embody the rest of it in the first paragraph, making it read this way:
Carriers by water shall be liable for the loss of or damage to goods except that they shall not be liable when such loss or damage happens without their actual fault or privity or without the fault or neglect of their agents, servants or employees.
Then striking out the word 'or' simply, and going on:
By reason of fire or the dangers of navigation; or, from any defect in or from the nature of the goods themselves; or, from armed robbery or other irresistible force.
It would bring section 964 back to read just as did read section 2 of chapter 82, R.S., 1886. If the hon. gentleman will look at that section in the Revised Statutes of 1906 he will see that it purports to reproduce section 2, of chapter 82, of 1886, but does not reproduce it. When I say purports to reproduce it also purports to revise, but in the process of revision they have altered the sense. It will bring it back to the original form of the statute.

In reply to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Doherty) I would say that he has altogether misunderstood me. I did not hold any threat over the hon. gentleman or anybody else. He has a perfect right to propose any amendment that he chooses to this Biil. I intend to vote against his amendment for two reasons, first, because it does not seem to me to be intelligible. The amendment renders the clause almost meaningless, because we all know that a ship-owner could not possibly be liable by his negligence for the acts of God, the King's enemies, and all those other things that are mentioned. Then, I intend to vote against his amendment for the further reason that I do not consider it is proper legislation. In my opinion, shipowners should not be liable for damage from fire, I care not how it was caused; they should not be liable for the whole value of the goods that are shipped. The ship-owner has always been able to make a contract up to this date. He does not consider whether the cargo that he takes on is valuable or not. It is not his cargo, he risks his own property and he undertakes to carry it and do the best he can, but it has hitherto been his privilege and right to make a contract that he will not be liable for the value of goods provided they are lost by fire at sea. I think that is a proper contract for him to make, and up to this date he has the right to make it under the law of Canada. Now we are taking that right away from him by section 4 of this Bill, ,and it ought to be conceded by every reasonable man, when we are taking that right away, that there are certain rights which we should leave with him. If we intend that shipping business is to be done, if we intend that capital shall go into shipbuilding, and if we are to be in the position of having our wheat, agricultural products and manufactured goods carried cheaply across the ocean, we must at least give the ship-owner the right to make a reasonable contract. It will be most unreasonable if the owner of the ship who loses his own property, a property, perhaps, worth a quarter of a million dollars, must also lose another quarter of a million dollars for the goods which have been lost. There is no reason why the clause should not be enacted as it stands. I beg to differ altogether from the hon. member for Montreal, Ste. Anne, with regard to that.

Bill (No. 198) to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act.-Mr. King-read a second time, and the House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
Will the minister give us some general light on this?

The proposed amendments are intended to simplify the procedure in the light of experience, and to meet what appears to be the very reasonable request made on the part of the working men through their organizations in respect to certain features of the Bill which they believe to operate to their disadvantage. The proposed amendments do not in any way change the principles of the Act as it stands. The Act has given general satisfaction during the three years of its existence, but the railway employees allege they are at a disadvantage as compared with the members of other labour organizations. For example, the Act requires that before a board of investigation is asked the parties must take an oath that the necessary authority to declare a strike or lockout has been obtained. Where the dispute is confined to one locality it is not difficult to secure this declaration, but where a dispute extends through various provinces, the railway men's organizations represent that the taking of a vote of their members is a great expense and inconvenience. The railway organizations have duly constituted grievance committees which take up grievances with the companies, and they claim they can get a long way in the settlement of differences by mutual conference, and that if they cannot succeed in that way the certainty of a vote being in favour of a strike is virtually established. Then, if the board is constituted after the vote has been taken before a strike can be declared, should the parties be unwilling to accept the findings of the board a second vote is required over the whole system, which also involves considerable expense. It is proposed by one of these amendments

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
to remedy that, and with proper safe-, guards, to allow the organizations to apply for a board if their officers can make a declaration to the effect that the difficulties between them and the company have already been the subject of careful negotiation and that they have got as far as is possible in the negotiations. A declaration to that effect the provisions of the Act in other particulars being complied with will be sufficient to warrant the government establishing a board.
There is one other point-under the law as it stands at present, if either of the parties change the conditions and the otheT party is not satisfied with the change of conditions, then before a strike or lockout can take place a board of investigation must be appointed. Experience in the working out of ithe Act has shown that while either party may change the conditions, in so far as employees iare concerned they must always make the application for a board. We are proposing an amendment here which will throw upon the party who proposes the change, the onus of asking for the board. In 'the ease of the strike of the machinists on the Canadian Pacific railway, in 1908, 'the company proposed certain changes which the men were not satisfied with, and before the men could go on strike they were obliged to ask for a board which reported adversely to them. It was then represented in the press that the men had asked for the board and refused to accept its findings. There is a slight element of injustice in that representation. The company having changed the conditions should have been obliged to call for the board before putting the changes into effect, and had that been the case it would not have appeared that the men were responsible for the calling of the board. There is an amendment framed which will remedy that state of things. I may say that I have submitted the amendments to the various railway brotherhoods, who are generally speaking the only parties that up to the present time have taken exception to the measure. The replies which have been received from them indicate that this proposed change removes the objection almost in whole, which any of them may have entertained towards the Act. I think it important to give this information to the committee, and with the permission of the House, I will Tead a communication which I sent to the duly authorized representatives of the different brotherhoods of railway employees, inclosing a copy of the proposed amendments and the replies that I have received :
Department of Labour, Canada,
Ottawa, March 5, 1910.
Dear Sir,-I am inclosing a copy of proposed amendments to the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, 1907, which have been

framed, after consultation with yourself and others, with a view of meeting what seem to me very reasonable requests made on behalf of the workingmen of this country through some of their representative labour bodies and officers, and in particular with a view of removing the possibilities of certain injustices which have been alleged on behalf of railway employees as existing, in so far as the provisions of the measure are applicable to them.
I wish you would kindly look carefully over the amendments proposed, and let me know whether in your opinion they are satisfactory, and whether if adopted by parliament they would bring the Industrial Disputes Act into a form generally satisfactory and acceptable to railway employees.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) W. L. MACKENZIE KING.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I might explain, that this Bill, although four or five pages in length, is very largely a Bill correcting and slightly amending some clauses of the present Fisheries Act. This section I, repeals subsection 4 of section 9 of the Fisheries Act, which reads: 'The holder of any such license shall not operate more than one whaling steamer in connection with the whale factory under license.' That particular section refers to the licensing of whale factories and the use of steamers. The custom hitherto on the Pacific coast has been to license factories about 100 miles apart, I think, and under the regulations the use of one steamer was permitted at one factory. By removing this clause, from the Act it will be possible for the minister to permit the use of two steamers at one factory. On the coast it has been found that sometimes whales were not numerous in the vicinity of one factory, and it was desired that the steamer attached to that factory might be used at another factory. The object of striking out this clause is to permit the use of two steamers at one factory, and when that is done, one of the factories will be closed up.
As a matter of fact, have not factories on the Pacific coast been using two steamers in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Not at all. A factory can only use one steamer under its license.
I know that, but I wanted to know whether the minister knew as a matter of fact that factories had been using two steamers, evading the law or having had permission given.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The department is not aware that the law has been evaded, and, of course, permission has not been given to evade the law.
On section 2, boundaries of estuary fishing.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I trust my hon. friend will not interpret my remarks as meaning that government measures will not be referred to that committee. As a matter of fact the department has received great assistance from that committee, and will avail itself of that assistance on every possible occasion.
Mr, R. L. BORDEN. 1 think the minister has not quite an adequate idea of the importance of the Bill in one respect at least. On section 15, the discussion of the regulations which have been agreed to should come up, and I would have thought it eminently proper that these regulations should be under investigation by the standing committee on Marine and Fisheries.
On section 7, closing of traps, &c., over Sunday.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The amendment is
in the last three lines, providing for the closing of these fishing apparatus in such a way that fish cannot enter. It strengthens the clause.

Does this mean that it will not be permitted to allow a trap net to remain set over Sunday? It has not been usual to prevent a fisherman from leaving his trap net set. It- is a very difficult net to move, it is large, it is put down with stakes, and anchors, and it is two days work to get the trap down. It would not be practicable to take it up over Sunday. I understand that this allows the closing of the trap so that no fish can get in on Sunday. What is the purpose of this amendment?
Does this Bill affect the international waters?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Clause 15 authorizes the department to take authority to proclaim the bringing into force of the fishery regulations established under the International Fisheries treaty.
The only change in clause 7 is to allow the effective closing of all traps during the weekly close season so that fish cannot enter them at all. It has been pointed out that the closing of pound nets is the method adopted in the state of Washington, and that the Same system has been used successfully in New Brunswick. It does not require the fishermen to remove the weirs or nets on Sunday, but simply to close them effectively.

The trouble we are having to understand this Bill simply shows that it should have been referred to the Fisheries Committee. It seems to me that the

object of the last three lines is to prevent the fishermen from desecrating the Sabbath. If this Bill had been referred to the Fisheries Committee, it would save this House bothering with it.

I suggest that the last three lines of this section will not help the case at all so far as they are intended
to preserve the fish from being taken in traps during the close season:
All sedentary fishing stations and weirs, all pounds and trap-nets, seines, gill-nets and other apparatus used for catching fish, whether under license or not, should be so raised or adapted as to admit of the free passage of fish through, by, or out of such apparatus, or be so effectively closed as to completely obstruct and prevent the entrance of fish into such apparatus.
If this matter had been referred* as suggested, to the Committee on Fisheries, I think that some members of that committee would have been able to show to the minister how that clause must fail of beneficial effect. While it provides that the traps themselves shall be closed, it makes no provision to prevent the fish getting into the leads, which are commonly about half a mile long, and into which the fish go and from which they do not return. So the effect of this provision is virtually to give continuous fishing to the traps. We have had experience of that in the past few years where the trap fishermen on Puget Sound have fished continuously because of a provision such as this. I know that the minister has in his department evidence of the effect of this provision on the Puget Sound traps, and I would ask him whether it would not be well to strike out the last three lines, and make this Act provide absolutely that there shall be free passage through the traps during the close season.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: My understanding of the effect of the statute as at present on the statute-book is that a fish trap has to be opened at one point in order to allow the fish to escape during the weekly close season. The addition provided by this amendment is that the entrance to the trap shall be closed so as completely to obstruct the entrance of the fish into the trap, and by preventing them from getting in, or permitting them when they are in to get out, during the weekly close season; that is what is contemplated by this amendment. That is the whole thing, it does not affect the hours of the close season. Previously, if fish got into the fish trap during the close season the trap was supposed to be open and the fish could get out. Under the present law the fish cannot be retained in the trap in the close season. _ The effect of this is to make it more difficult during the close season for fish to get into the traps.

I wrould like to know if this applies to fishing on the Atlantic coast as well as to British Columbia? It appears to me that it applies to all waters. It strikes me this is rather a stringent rule to impose upon the fisherman owning a trap, that during the prohibited hours from six o'clock in the afternoon of every Saturday to six o'clock on Monday morning in t'dal waters, fishing cannot Ije allowed, and that the net must not be opened at all during those hours. That is a new provision, that I never heard of before, and I think it will take away a very valuable privilege from the trap fishermen that they now possess. On the Atlantic coast there are a great number of them.
The hon. member is quite mistaken as to its being a new provision, it is a provision of the law now. The only change in this clause is in the phraseology, that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This has been the law for years. The clause is the same as it is in the present Act, except the last three lines, which simply make it more difficult for the fish to get into the trap; that is the only change we are making. We are simply trying to limit the catching of fish in traps during the present close season-we are not changing the close season at all. We are trying to make the Act more effective, and trying to make a regulation that will prevent the fish from getting into the trap, and to allow them the chance to get out if they should get in. The law contemplates that there shall be during every week a close season, and it is because the present fixtures in the trap are not perfect, and because the fish are caught in traps and retained there, and the aperture is not open for them to get out-those are the reasons the department has thought it advisable to say that the fishermen must effectually close their traps so that the fish cannot get in. There can be no doubt of the necessity for conserving the fish by permitting them to have one day's rest at all events, so that no trap or net will take them. This has been the law for years and years. It may not have been effective, and it may not be under this amendment properly enforced, but that is the intention. We want to make it a little more possible to enforce the law.

I do not think the minister has answered the contention raised by my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor). This lead is from half a mile to three-quarters of a mile long, and while the trap may be closed the lead practically holds all the fish there, and as soon as the trap is opened fish which have congregated all Sunday will move into the trap. It is absolutely necessary in the interest of the fisheries that the'fish should

have free passage one day in a week. If the fishery department wants to make this law effective there must be more than the closing of the trap; the lead must be closed also.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I quite understand that the point raised is important particularly on the Pacific coast. The leads leading up to the traps in the Pacific ocean are very long, and no doubt keep back a large number of fish. I may say, however, that nine-tenths of the Canadian salmon caught in traps in the Pacific ocean are caught in American traps on the American side of the boundary, and that there these leads are in use. We have in British Columbia very few traps indeed, not a quarter as many as they have on the American side. I am informed that this amendment that we are putting into the Fishery Act, and which will apply to all Canada, was approved of by the Fishery Commission, and will apply also to the traps on the Pacific ocean. This is an attempt to make the taking of fish in traps during the close season more difficult than formerly. In the fishery regulations which have been drafted by the fishery Commissioners of Canada and the United States, there are some regulations in Tegard to trap fishing and this is one of the provisions of these regulations. This is the best we can do as between Canadian and American fishermen in regard to international waters. It is a very desirable addition to this clause. I am sure that what the House and every person interested in the fisheries wants is to conserve the fisheries, and if there is a close season for one day in the week, which may be Sunday or any other day, the whole object and intention is to make that closed day effective so that fish will not be taken in traps.

I agree with the minister that everybody who has any interest in the fisheries, must admit that there should be one day in the week during which fish cannot be taken, but I contend that the contention raised by my hon. friend from New Westminster is absolutely correct, that as long as these trap nets are allowed to remain in the water, and these long leads are allowed to remain down while the trap is not catching fish, the fish are congregating there, and when the trap is opened next day the fish that would have passed through, if the lead had been opened or up, will simply find their way into the trap. I can understand very well that this amendment is a step in the right direction, but I contend that it does not go far enough. The leads to the trap nets should be lifted during the day when fishing is not allowed. If that had been taken up with the International Commission it should have been arranged, because I
understand that on the coast the Americans are really getting our Canadian fish. The amendments you are proposing I do not think will be effective to a very great extent as far as protecting our fish are concerned. While you do not fish on Sunday the fish are congregating there and they will go into the trap on Monday.

I wnuld like to point out that the addition which the minister has made to the section renders it absolutely inoperative in so far as providing a weekly closed season is concerned, and that before he added anything to it it was an effective provision. It was provided that the fish should pass freely through the traps at all times. Now, it simply erects a barrier against which the fish may congregate while the trap is not supposed to be in operation and where they will remain until the hour comes for the lifting of the gate of the trap when all the fish will go in and be caught- The remedy is very simple. If the government does not think it wise to provide that there must be a free passageway through the traps, there is another device by which they can effect a close season and that is to provide that there shall be an opening in the lead through which the fish will pass when they find their way barred by the gate of the trap. The International Fisheries Commission recognized that when they were dealing with fish other than the salmon of the Pacific coast. Unfortunately it is true that the provision that they have made with regard to Pacific coast salmon is not effective. We seem to have deferred to the American greed for the catching of fis'h without Tespect to the effect on the industry, and we have allowed them to make a provision with respect- to the Puget Sound for continuous fishing. But, with regard to Ontario, they have made an effective regulation which I see no reason for not applying to the Pacific coast. The Ontario regulation reads as follows:
During this weekly close season, all weirs or other fitted apparatus used for the capture of salmon shall be so raised, closed, or adapted as to admit of the free passage of fish through, or by, or out of such weirs or other fixed apparatus.
There is an effective provision. What I want to know is why we cannot have a provision so simple and so effective as that under the general operation of the law so that it may apply to the traps in Ontario, the maritime province and British Columbia alike.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I think that a careful perusal of this section will show that exactly what the hon. member for New Westminster wants is provided for. The trap may be either closed or opened, which-1 ever way is the more effective.
The trap?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The trap may be either opened or closed:
It shall he so raised or adapted as to admit of the free passage of fish through, by, or out of such apparatus, or he so effectively closed as to completely obstruct and prevent the entrance of fish into such apparatus, whether under license or not.
Is it at the option of the trap operator or the fishery officer that it shall be opened or closed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This amendment is recommended by the British Columbia Fishery Commission.
At whose option is this?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I am stating that this amendment is on the recommendation of the British Columbia	Fish
Commission. The same regulation has been adopted by the American commissioner in the state of Washington. It would seem to me from the reading of the clause, that it will be at the option of the party operating the trap, and I would at once concede to my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Taylor) that if the House thinks it desirable to make it at the option of the fishery inspector I am prepared to do so The most effective way to close the trap is to have it at the option of the fishery overseer, who will see that the trap is open or closed as the case may be.
If the minister makes it at the option of the fishery inspector and not the trap operator, for myself I can see no objection to it.

In that is involved the important question that our legislation on the Canadian side should be uniform with the American legislation. Unfortunately, for many years the Americans have always got the best of us in this respect, and if we make our law stringent and allow the Americans to have theirs as lax as they like, they will get the salmon and we wont. The concession which the minister offers to make is undoubtedly a proper one, but if we make our fishery officer responsible for seeing that the traps should be opened or closed then there should be some pressure brought to bear on the American authorities to have a similar regulation on their side. We have been protecting the fish in Canadian waters, but the Americans have been fishing how and when they like, and that is a great hardship to Canadian fishermen. If we cannot induce the American fish commissioners to meet our Canadian regulations, then a good deal of our work for fish preservation is useless.
If this Bill is of such a simple character as the minister has stated,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: and if we have had practically the same law on the statute-book for a great many years, no interest can suffer by allowing the Bill to stand over for another session, and referring it to the fisheries commission, so that we may ascertain the conditions both here and in the United States, and try to make uniform the regulations of both countries.

How would this legislation affect the regulations issued by the National Fisheries Commissioners in respect to fishing in international waters? I presume that the regulations made by that commission, being the result of a treaty, will have priority over any law we may pass.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Taylor) will see the force of the observations of the hon. member for Selkirk, that it would be discriminatory to make more drastic regulations on the Canadian side than exist on the American side. The International Fisheries Commissioners have agreed to certain regulations, and this regulation now proposed is the regulation on the American side. If, as I proposed, we should make this provision enforcible by the Canadian inspector on the Canadian side, and the American inspectors on the American side have not the enforcement of it, we would be subjecting our fishermen to more stringent regulations than the Americans would operate under. Perhaps it is better to leave this clause as it is. We are working under extraordinary difficulties, particularly on the Pacific coast, with regard to our fisheries. The Americans catch our fish when passing through their waters, as they have a perfect right to do, and they catch them in their own way. They have been catching fish for a great many years in traps without comparatively speaking any regulations at all, while we on our side have been enforcing stringent regulations. Under the proposed agreement with the United States, what are practically the Canadian regulations 'have been adopted by the International Commission, and they will be enforced so soon as they are proclaimed the law on both sides.
This Bill would in no way limit the conclusions arrived at by that commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No.

I have a doubt whether the traps used on the Atlantic coast are capable of being closed. I am not a practical fisherman, but I have seen the traps, and as I understand it there is no machinery for closing them, so that you would require a trap differently constructed from that now used in order to comply with this regulation.

I sympathize with the Minister of Fisheries in the difficulty in which he is placed, for I think it must be admitted that he has at last let the cat out of the bag. We are not in this section doing anything to help to conserve the salmon, but we are facing the position that by our international agreement with the Americans we have sanctioned their deliberate intention to have no close season so- far as traps are concerned; and having sanctioned that, we have amended our own law so that we shall not do on the Canadian side of the boundary what toy international agreement we sanctioned on the other side. I think this is a most deplorable condition, a condition that is bound to work great hardship on the great mass of Canadians engaged in the salmon fishery industry to the extent that we are relaxing the law and_ giving sanction to continuous trapfishing by the section now proposed. We should strenuously refuse to make any change in our law, but should insist upon our regulation, which experience has shown to be so advisable, to the extent, if necessary, of allowing these international regulations to fall to the ground because of the reluctance of this parliament to adopt them. I say that in all seriousness, because so far as we on the Pacific coast are concerned, we are apt to experience nothing but calamity from the operation of those regulations. On every point they are against us, most seriously against us. I will not discuss them now, because they come in under section 15; but there are other sections quite as disastrous to us as this section 7, which in two lines destroys the only prohibition we have had in the past against continuous trap fishing.
On section 9, fish guards ini British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Northwest territories and Yukon.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This is the clause as it stands at present that the words 'British Columbia' are introduced, making the law applicable to that province.

I do not know that there is any other clause in this Bill which will give me the opportunity of drawing the minister's attention to tire fact that in the construction of the dam on the Red river at St. Andrew's rapids there is no provision for a [DOT] fishway. This is a very serious trouble. The dam is situated 25 or 30 miles from Lake Winnipeg, and completely prevents the fish from getting up the river. I had the matter before the Fsheries Department, and I had the assurance of the deputy that immediate action would be taken and a proper fishway placed there. During the time the Minister of Public Works was oassing his estimates, I called his attention to the matter, 255
but the only assurance I received from him was that if a fishway were found necessary it would be placed there. I think it is absolutely necessary, because at present no fish from Lake Winnipeg can pass up the Red river or the Assinaboine. I would urge the minister to see that a proper fishway is provided there immediately.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I quite agree with what my hon. friend says. This clause has nothing to do with fishways; but if the ascent of the fish up the Red river is prevented by the dam. there should be an adequate fishway provided. We have many instances of the same kind in British Columbia, where dams have been erected and have stopped the passage of fish. I am a strong believer in allowing the free run of fish on all rivers. Natural spawning after all is better than artificial, and ought to be encouraged. The officer of the department lias informed me that the matter to which my hon. friend has referred is receiving the consideration of the department now.
On section 11, standard size of oyster barrel.
Mr.' TEMPLEMAN. I move to strike out section 11. 6ome legislation is required to standardize the size of barrels for various purposes, hut it belongs to the Trade and Commerce Department rather than to the Fisheries Department. Not having full information as to what the standard of a barrel of oysters should be, it has been decided to leave the matter over for this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I am advised that the matter is one for the province of Quebec. The fishery is under their control, and the taking of this fish comes under the regulations of the province of Quebec and not under the regulations of the Dominion government. I may also inform my hon. friend that the matter has been the subject of correspondence between the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the province of Quebec, and there is some reasonable prospect of an arrangement whereby the bar fish will be protected more than it has been in the past.
