House in committee on Bill (No. 210) to incorporate the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada.-Mr. Gervais.
On section 1,

I would like a few words of explanation on this Bill. I had not the privilege of being present at the meetings of the committee except on one occasion when a Bill somewhat similar to this was up for discussion, and was, I believe, opposed very strenuously by the same gentlemen who are seeking incorporation under this Bill. I refer to the co-operative Bill which was killed in committee, largely I believe by reason of the strong fight put up against it by the Retailers' Association. What a good many cannot understand is how it is that the Retail Merchants' Association fought that Bill so strenuously, and refused incorporation to the consumers, whereas they are themselves seeking incorporation for a somewhat similar purpose in the Bill now before the House. Grain Growers Guide which voices the opinion of Mr. TALBOT.
the farmers, the consuming population very largely in the west, says':
The Retail Merchante' Association did not want to see the co-operative Bill pass^ the House of Commons. They wanted it killed, and it was killed. The Bill would have allowed consumers throughout Canada to organize among themselves for fair play if they so desired, and would protect them against unjust prices on the part of all dealers. This Bill being killed leaves the consumers in the same helpless condition as they were before. The Retail Merchants' Association is getting busy, and has a Bill before the Senate to incorporate itself to do business. This is certainly 'doing things' with a vengeance. The consumers of Canada may not be allowed to co-operate, _ but the retail merchants want to become incorporated so that they can form a trust similar to the one existing in the United States. Down across the line it is considered that the retailers are more to blame for the high cost of living than probably any other organization. Are we going to sit by and see them do the same thing in Canada? We doubt if the farmers and consumers will stand for this.
I am not in a position to vouch for the accuracy of every statement contained in this paragraph, but I would like some explanation from the promoter to explain away some of these statements if they can be explained away. The accusation here made against the Retailers' Association would seem reasonable, that having objected to the incorporation of the Co-operative Society under that Bill, they are seeking under this Bill extensive powers which they would deny to the consuming population. In another issue of the Grain Growers ' Guide,' appears this article:
The Refail Merchants' Association has been successful in killing the co-operative Bill before the House of Commons. This is the Bill that would have allowed the consumers of Canada to do their own business and protect themselves from exorbitant prices on the part of the retailers. Following up their victory the retail merchants have now a Bill before the Senate to provide for their own incorporation. This will give them the powers of a trust, as one of the powers given by the Bill is: 'the promotion of the industrial and commercial interests of the retail merchants of Canada,' and another is: ' generally, all such other lawful objects for promoting the trade interests of its members as may from time to time be determined by the association '.
As will be seen by this clause they are very indefinite in their terms, and the Bill may cover great powers. I would like an explanation of the details to which I have drawn attention.

I do not see how there can be confusion between the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, and the Cooperative Societies which some of the hon. members would have liked to have seen

formed under an Act introduced in this House. The co-operative societies of which the hon. gentleman has just spoken were commercial societies trying to benefit themselves commercially to the utter detriment of other classes, and of the masses of the country. These co-operative societies in a general way were purely and simply commercial societies, organized for the purpose of trespassing on the ground of the consumers of trespassing on the ground of the retail merchants, and on the ground of the wholesale merchants of Canada. If I am allowed to define the object of this society, I will be able to show that the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada is more a philanthropic than a commercial society. The contrary was proved in reference to the so-called co-operative societies of Canada, for which incorporation was sought from this House. Let me quote for example from section 2 of the present Bill, defining the objects of our society:
The objects of the association shall he the promotion of the industrial and commercial interests of the retail merchants of Canada.
I may assure you that the Retail Merchants Association of Canada are not trying to derive financial benefit from the good work they wish to be enabled to do in the interests of all, because I think the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada as well as the wholesale merchants of Canada have done more for the progress, and the prosperity of Canada than any other class.
No, no.

Yes, yes. If Montreal is something more than a little village, it is due to the marvellous audacity and tenacity of its wholesale and retail merchants, and the same remark may be made applicable to all the cities of our country. I shall try to explain to you in a few words what has been done in the past in relation to the promotion of the industrial and commercial interests by the retail merchants of Canada. For instance they have dealt with the abolishing of. trading stamps, coupons in packages, and of all lotteries and merchandizing schemes; the adjustment of taxation, both municipal and provincial; the regulating of the hours of closing; advising and consulting on city by-laws regarding awnings, clean streets, the regulation of signs, &c. That has been one part of the work which the Retail Merchants' Association has been doing for fourteen years, for that society was incorporated fourteen years ago. Let me also say the association has been promoting all that time fair adjustments of freight rates, express charges, increase and decrease of duties on parcel posts; prosecuting fraudulent advertisements and sales, and adulterations of goods. The association has been also pub-255}
lishing information and statistics relating to, or concerning trade interests, such as supplying the Dominion government with the number of retail merchants doing business in Canada, the amount of their investments therein, the taxes paid by them, their employees and the amount of goods sold for cash or credit. This information is not supplied officially in any department from other sources.
Let me now speak of the arbitration and settlement of trade disputes between any of it3 members. For instance, the farmers who produced milk met not long ago, and they made a hard and fast rule that unless the retail milk dealers bought milk at their price that they would simultaneously cut off all milk supplies by them in Toronto, and the retail milk dealers appealed to their members, and the latter decided to arbitrate, which was done, and it resulted in a fair, compromise, so that the farmer, the retailer and the consumer received fair treatment. The working tailors also decided to strike, and their case was settled by the association, and entire harmony now exists among them. They have settled also disputes with regard to whether merchants sold the quality of goods to their customers that they represented them to be, also a great many other technical trade matters.
The procuring and furnishing to its members of information as to the solvency of persons who deal with any of its members. For instance, it is estimated that about 75 per cent of the retail sales made from day to day are made on credit. This means an enormous sum of money, and no matter how the condition is viewed, this system in my opinion, will continue, as it is more convenient for the housekeeper, and in many cases for the storekeeper, especially when orders are sent in, as a great many now are, over the telephone. There are some people who make it a practice to live on the storekeepers, and they have no moral sense of what is right. In many casesj workingmen are out of work, especially in-the winter time; others are absolutely hon-j est and they meet with misfortune-to all these credit is extended, but those who deceive us are placed on a list, and if they will not pay, and it is thought they should, this acts as an incentive for them to be honest. The deserving ones are assisted through the organized associated charities, which are mostly conducted and contributed to by the retail merchants. Where-ever possible they put themselves in touch with the ministers, preachers and priests and rectors of parishes regarding' these people, and they have helped hundreds to help themselves.
' Generally, all other lawful and similar objects for promoting the trade interests of its members as may from time to time be determined by the association.' This clause

applies to all of the preceding, and the words ' lawful and similar,' in our opinion, is quite sufficient to safeguard all concerned. No possible danger can come out of this charter, as everything that is acted upon must be first voted upon, and in the association are some of the most upright men in the community, men who are looked up to by the people and who occupy public positions such as mayors, reeves, magistrates, justices of the peace-men who hold high positions in the churches, on school boards and in other public capacities, and it would, therefore, he almost impossible to' get them to impose upon the community anything that was unfair, and especially upon the consumers, who are their friends and customers. All the other clauses refer to the details regarding the rules of the association. I admit that they have been trying to do something in the interest of the retail merchants, but, their efforts have been more especially in the interests of the consumers and the general public. You will see by paragraph (b) of section 2 that the association asks for power to collect and publish information and statistics relating to or concerning such interests. Well, you will find in the work of the association that it has been for 14 years supplying the Dominion government with statistics as to the number of retail merchants who are doing business in Canada the amount of money invested, the taxes paid, and the sales on cash and for credit. I shall not detain the House by defining what is done under each of these paragraphs of section 2; I say they show in a summary way what are the aims and objects of this association. I think I have said enough to demonstrate that the association is more a benevolent than a commercial society, and that there is no danger to any class in the country or to the public interest in the little Bill which is now before the House.

Will the hon. gentleman tell us why this association needs to be incorporated by an Act of this parliament for the purposes which are .set out in the Bill. According to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gervais) this is a voluntary association which has been carrying on this beneficial work for a number of years, and why then do they want an Act of incorporation from this parliament?

The answer is that the 'Retail Merchants' Association of Canada was incorporated 14 years ago bv a statute of the Ontario legislature, and, the Ontario association has been promoting its objects throughout the different provinges. but in some cases they have been con fronted with the fact that the local associa ion will not pay anything towards the good work. The Ontario association was al-Mr. GERVAIS.
ways of the opinion that it would be more fitting that a general association should be formed under the charter of which the local branches should be forced to do their work when they are willing to enter the general association. This is merely the 'incorporation of a few retail merchants' associations for the benefit of all.
Why don't you seek incorporation under the provincial law?
Trade and commerce are regulated by the parliament of Canada, and if the association is chartered by this parliament they will be better enabled to carry on their work.
But this is not trade and commerce, it is a benevolent association.
Our association does not intend to do any trade or to interfere with the business of anybody in the land; it is simply a benevolent society.

I do not know that anybody can take serious objection to the incorporation of a retail merchants' association as a Dominion institution, but it is important to point out to the House that the very gentleman who led the attack against the incorporation of co-operative societies in this House, is the very gentleman who is promoting the incorporation of this retail .merchants' association. And the same corporation that engaged that gentleman to do that work in their interests at that time are evidently employing him at the present time.

I rise to a point of order. I wish to tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith) that I never was retained by the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada to do such work. What I am doing is I believe, in the public interest.

I said that the hon. gentleman was engaged by the Retail Merchants' Association to promote their interests against the Co-operation Bill. I would not suspect that my hon. friend would for one moment be retained further than that he was willing to use his influence to -combat the principle of co-operation in the interests of the retail merchants' association. Now, I would point out that every reason which the hon. gentleman (Air. Gervais) gave against the Co-operative Bill is given by him now as a reason in support of this Bill. He argued that the Co-operative Society should be incorporated in the several provinces, Jhat it was not a Dominion organization, that it should not be recognized as a Dominion corporation, that it should be continued as a provincial work and so on. I rvould also point out to the hon. gentleman, and every one of these applies

to his retail merchants' association, that this Bill provides that the retail merchants association shall hold real property, and that it shall carry on business in other respects.

The fact is that section 6 of this Bill has only one purpose, namely, to enable the corporation to purchase and hold property notwithstanding the laws of mortmain. We are bound by the enactment of mortmain in this country, and to get over that even a benevolent society has to be authorized by parliament to possess real estate. As a matter of fact, the hon. gentleman cannot find in section 6 anything which tends to show that the Retail ^Merchants' Association of Canada intends to engage in any kind of trading. They simply want to be empowered to possess real property, the amount of which is strictly limited by the section.

Section 6 of this Bill provides, that this association may carry on all kinds of business, and the same provision in the Co-operation Bill was vigorously opposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Gervais). It does seem to me that the Co-operative Society was much more entitled to do a Dominion business between its own members than this society to deal with the general public. The same hon. gentleman who is promoting this Bill did everything he could to prevent the co-operative movement. Section 7 of this Bill provides for the acquisition of property of voluntary associations, and that means that this incorporated body is getting power to provide for the purchase of the societies that may not be able to exist when the organization of this society is completed. The provisions of section 7 give the necessary power to acquire property to a society that may not be able to operate as a consequence of this organization, and therefore, you create a practical monopoly of the Retail Grocers' Association. My hon. friend may shake his head, but; there is the section that provides for the possession of that property. I have no serious objection to the incorporation of any society of this kind, but it is a very unfair thing for a responsible member of this House to object all he could to the organization of a voluntary institute that sought powers from this parliament simply to do business with its own members, when he is now in favour of granting far more extensive Powers to an organization that seeks to do business with the whole country. *

This seems a very extraordinary Bill to bring in towards the close of this session in view of what occurred somewhat earlier in connection with those co-operative Bills that have been mentioned by my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith). My hon. friend (Mr. Gervais)
who is supporting this Bill has not . made clear to my mind any good reason why the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada ought to be incorporated by an Act of this parliament. As my hon. friend from Nanaimo has said, the same hon. gentleman opposed the formation of co-operative societies that merely had in view the mutual benefit of their own members, taking as one of his grounds that the provinces should deal with a matter of that kind. But, if the objects of this association are as innocent as my hon. friend stated, it seems to me that "he has given no reason, no ground whatever, why this Bill should be put through this House. They have been carrying on practically all the work they propose to carry on under the terms of section 2 of this Bill as a voluntary association, and I see a lurking menace in this Bill against the interests of the consumers of this country. It seems to me that this Retail Merchants' Association, if it is incorporated in this way, might become a monopoly. We have spent a great deal of time in this House, to-day, and on other days, in- passing a Bill with which to protect the consumers of this country from monopolies and trusts. I do not see any reason, if this association is incorporated by Act of parliament, why it may not become a menace to the consumers of Canada in so far as the regulation of retail prices is concerned. The promoter of the Bill may say that this cannot be, that the Bill that we have already put through the House will prevent it, but there are ways and means-underground wavs and means-whereby these incorporated associations are able to do things, and it is very difficult- to find them out or catch them in the act. One of the subsections of section 2 gives another object of this association as the arbitration and settlement of trade disputes arising between any of its members. We have an Industrial Disputes Act on the statute-books already. I do not know that we ought to delegate to the Retail Grocers' Association any such powers as this whatever. It seems to me that a general Act dealing with that question is quite sufficient. The co-operative Bills that were before this House some time ago were smothered in committee. I was not a member of the committee that dealt with those Bills, and I regret very much that the Bills were not reported to the House. I say frankly that I am opposed to this Bill. I am opposed to it for one reason besides those which I have already given, and that is because this very retail grocers' association were the people who were practically instrumental in the defeat of the co-operative societies Bills. I believe those Bills were in the interest of the consumers, the farmers and the workingmen of this country, and yet we had a large delegation of

these retail grocers and other retail tradesmen of this Dominion who came here and brought every influence to bear on the committee that dealt with these Bills for the purpose of smothering them. They were smothered, and I say that it is only fair that this Bill, which is introduced by the people who are responsible for the destruction of the other Bills, should be accorded like treatment and sent to oblivion along with the co-operative societies Bills.

I must say a word in answer to a statement of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Neely). It is rather a queer argument to say that we must kill this Bill because another Bill has been considered bad by the House or by one of its committees. I have not had a long experience in parliamentary life, but I know enough to say that each measure must be adjudicated upon with reference to its own individual merits and not with reference to a question of personality or of individuality which has nothing to do with the measure.
What about precedent?

There is no precedent. The Co-operative Bill was justly killed because it was against the public interest. It was so considered by the Committee on Banking and Commerce, and every other Bill which contains provisions which are regarded as a menace to the trade of the country will be considered in a similar way. But here we have a Bill in which *a very important class of people are simply seeking for incorporation and nothing else. It is idle to assert that through this Bill there is any intention of doing any trade, and more especially of creating any kind of monopoly. Any gentleman who has any experience in business or of the law will support my contention that through this Bill the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada are merely asking for a charter of incorporation. I will leave It to the interpretation of any lawyer or business man of unbiased mind. Fortunately or unfortunately I have been fighting the Cooperative Bill. I did it because I had had sufficient experience to convince me that it was a bad Bill, and it was so held unanimously by the members of the Banking and Commerce Committee. I say this is a good Bill, that it is a Bill that is in accordance with the public laws, that it is a Bill which is in accordance with the constitution of 1867, and that it is a Bill which should pass, as we are bound to give any charter in answer to any demand which is made upon this House in accord-ace with the laws of the country and in accordance more especially with the rules of equity and justice.

I may say that if there was a possibility of this association * Mr. NEELY.
going into trade, I would feel like my hon. friend from Humbolt (Mr. Neely), but if it is simply an institution that we are incorporating the same as we might incorporate the butchers' association, or the wholesale grocers' association, or the com exchange, or any other exchange of that kind, there can be no objection to it. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gervais) says it is not to carry on trade of any kind there can be no objection to it.

The powers which this company are applying for here can be acquired by them under the provisions of the Ontario Company's Act. I had for a time charge of the administration of the Ontario Company's Act, and my impression is that the powers asked for here may be obtained by order of the Lieutenant Governor in Council. This is purely a matter which should come under the jurisdiction of the different provinces, and if this association desires to exceed the boundaries of any particular province they can obtain registration and do business in the different provinces of the Dominion. This is certainly not a Bill which should be enacted in this parliament.

There is another feature of this Bill to which I wish to call the attention of the promoter. I know that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gervais) is very plausible in his plea that this retail association is a purely philanthropic institution, but I draw 'his attention to a very innocent little subclause (a) of section (3) which says:
The association may make by-laws for: (a) the administration, management and control of the property, business, and other affairs of the association.
Now. in the Act for the incorporation of the Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Timiskaming which passed this House this session, there was an almost word foT word subclause which read:

If the hon. gentleman is willing to accept such an amendment as that, for my

part I am willing with that safeguard to let go through this innocent Bill for a benevolent purpose, as he describes it to be. I join issue with the non. member (Mr. Roche) on the ground that the amendment incorporated in the other Bill was useless, because any corporation which does anything not authorized by its charter would be compelled to desist by a writ of quo warranto issued upon information. I would like to ask the hon. member why he requires clause 0 which reads:
The association may receive, acquire, accept and hold real property by gift, purchase, devise, bequest, lease or otherwise, for the purposes of the association, and may sell, lease, invest or otherwise dispose thereof in such manner as it may deem advisable for such purposes: Provided, however, that the annual value of the real estate held by the association shall not exceed the sum of fifty thousand dollars.
Now, $50,000 per annum is a large amount of real estate for an ordinary association formed for benevolent purposes to hold. The phrase ' the purposes of the association '[DOT] in that clause may be very widely construed. I would like to correct the hon. member for Humboldt in his reference to the Co-operation Bill. was considered to be impossible as drawn and that is why it was thrown out.

All legitimate powers sought for by this society can be Obtained under the joint stock companies Acts of the different provinces. Some of the powers they apply for here would not he given them in the provinces, and why should we interfere with the rights of the provinces by .incorporating this company here. I am quite satisfied in my own mind that this legislation has some otheT purpose than that which appears on the face of it. They can obtain all the power necessary for carrying on legitimate business from the provincial secretaries of the different provinces.

If we allow this Bill to go through, it will give these people power to form the largest combine that has ever been known in Canada. I am a retail merchant myself, and I am satisfied that this Bill will give the retail merchants power to form themselves into associations to restrict the number of stores in each little town throughout the whole country. They will be able to control prices and to restrict trade all over Canada. The hon. gentleman who has introduced the Bill says that the wholesale people of Montreal are practically a benevolent society. I want to say that I have bought thousands of dollars worth of goods from the wholesale people of Montreal, and I have never seen any sign of that so far.

Mr. GUTHRIE moved the second reading of Bill (No. 218), respecting the Guelph Junction Railway Company.-Mr. Clarke (Essex).
I would ask the hon. gentleman who has charge of the Bill to make some explanation of it. I think it calk for some explanation.
I understand that the promoter is not here.
Then the hon. member for South Wellington had better ask that the Bill stand.

I am not in charge of the Bill, but it is one that affects the constituency that I have the honour to represent, and I think it ought certainly to go to the Railway Committee. That committee meets on Thursday, and it is just possible that it may not have another meeting this session. 1 do not know another instance in which a private Bill has stood under such circumstances, and I would ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw his request, and let the Bill go to the committee and be considered there. It is a Bill that has already passed the Senate. If a brief statement is wanted, 1 think I could perhaps outline the situation. This is a Bill practically in the interest of the city of Guelph, whereby that city asks for the right to take over all stock in this company which may be outstanding. The city of Guelph is practically the owner of a small road sixteen miles long, running from the city to the Canadian Pacific railway, constructed by the city of Guelph in 1888 at a cost of about a quarter of a million dollars, at the request of a number of gentlemen who claimed that they must have competition, as we had only the Grand Trunk railway at Guelph at that time. It was necesary that some men should qualify to be directors, and ten men took ten shares each in the common stock of the company, on which they paid $100 each. It turned out that the road cost more than was anticipated, and the city asked that the ten gentlemen should pay up the balance on their shares, which they refused to do, claiming that they held the stock as trustees for the city. The ratepayers finally passed a by-law to pay the indebtedness and relieve the shareholders from payment of the balance upon their Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
stock and the stock-holders agreed to hold their stock as trustees for the city. The city assented to this, but allowed them to hold one share each and continue on the board. The road is indebted yet in respect of its bonds to the extent of between $60,Uuu and $70,000, but since it has been continued to Goderich by the Canadian Pacific railway it has become a very good earning proposition for the city of Guelph. Four or live of the shares originally held by these trustees are still outstanding. All the others have transferred their interests to the city and have received their $100 and $300 by way of bonus-$400 in all for the $100 that they had paid. Four or five have refused to hand over their shares, and this Bill, I understand, is to compel the transfer of these shares on the payment of the sum of $400 and also to permit the' city to issue stock to represent the $70,000 of indebtedness still on the bonds.
Originally who paid for these shares?
The individuals who subscribed $100 each.
The individuals subscribed and paid.

They subscribed $100; the city then relieved them of $19,000 of indebtedness, and of the $900 which each was liable to pay on their call on signing the declaration that they held the shares as trustees for the city.
Then you are asking for the right to confiscate other people's property?

I do not look upon it as confiscation. 1 have gone into the matter very carefully, and I am satisfied it is right. I think it would be far better to discuss it when the shareholders are before the committee, as they will be on Thursday.

In consenting to the second reading of this Bill we are necessarily adopting its principle, and in adopting the principle of this Bill we are adopting a very pernicious principle in respect to the legislation of this House. Let us look at clause 2, irrespective of any collateral circumstances.

I do not like to interrupt my hon. friend, but I am sure he wants to give thi3 Bill fair treatment. There are only a few minutes left now, and there is only one' more sitting before we prorogue. If he is reasonable at all he will allow it to go to the committee.

I do not like to have it insinuated that I am not giving this Bill fair treatment. I may say I do not think it was very fair treatment on the part of my

hon. friend t-o slip in a motion to suspend the rule so as t-o get rid of the 24 hours' notice we ought to have had. This Bill was only introduced to the House last night for the first time.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. I never heard of a motion of that kind until now.

This Bill was only read the first time last night, and but for the suspension of the rule, to the motion respecting which I fancy nobody paid any attention, my hon. friend would not be here to-night at all. Therefore, I do not think he can complain of any reasonable criticism upon his Bill, and I do not think 1 deserve, out of the mouth of my hon. friend,, any 3uch comment or charge that I have been obstructing or opposing any Bill which did not deserve, for some reason or another, to be opposed. I am speaking to the principle of the Bill, that principle' which we are now asked to accept, and 1 want to say that if we commit ourselves to the principle of this Bill, we are committing ourselves to a very dangerous principle indeed, because as my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said, we virtually say to this minority of shareholders, those shareholders mentioned in section 2, you have got to sell your shares and you have got to deliver those shares at the valuation which parliament _ places upon them, irrespective of what their value may be to them in the future. Now, my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) himself has taken strong grounds with respect to the very same shares and to this very railway, grounds diametrically opposed to the legislation asked for under section 2. I propose to demonstrate that to him and then to satisfy him that I am not unnecessarily commenting upon what I conceive to be ,a pernicious principle in this Bill. What is the principle to which we are asked to subscribe? The corporation of the city of Guelph may, subject to the laws of Ontario, acquire any shares in the company not now standing in the name of the city, and the said corporation is hereby empowered and declared to be entitled to acquire the said shares of the company's stock from the several persons in whose names the shares stand or may stand, and to have transfers thereof made by such persons respectively to the said corporation upon payment to such person respectively of the sum of $400 in respect of each one share fully paid up, or of each ten shares, upon which ten per cent only has been paid; and it shall be the duty of such persons respectively to transfer such shares to the said corporation accordingly. Now, speaking for myself, I cannot subscribe to any such principle as that, that part can take any beneficial ownership of shares or of
any property as that section empowers that company to do, and say, here is your $4UO for that 3tock, though it may be worth a, thousand dollars, and I believe that each, one of those shares is approximately worth $1,000. But whether it be worth only $400 or $450 a share, have we the right as a parliament, and if we have the right, should it be exercised in this way, to compel the shareholders of that company, who are not trustees, but who are beneficially entitled to their own shares, to give those shares-up? My hon. friend himself says that nobody wanted to take their shares away from them, that their shares were their own.
I say, can he come nine years later and say, that which I said we did not want to take away, I now want to take away. I say this is an interference with the rights of property. It i3 an interference with civil rights. It is an interference with the right of a party to retain his own shares.

House in committee on Bill (No. 192) to amend the Fisheries- Act.
On section 12,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The only change in, this section is that the return asked for should be sent to the minister through the inspector of fisheries for the district not later than the 31st day of May of each year, instead of not later than the 1st day of September, as in the Fisheries Act.
On section 13,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The change in this clause is- simply the addition of the words-in the 24th and 28th line3 ' or of any international regulation.'

It does seem that this Bill covers a great deal of ground, and we should have some lucid explanation o-f the whole matter. I cannot understand why the minister having the Bill in charge should come before this committee, and ask us to pass it without having sent it to the Committee on Fisheries. It seems a complicated Bill, and the further we get the more complicated it gets. There must be something in it or the Bill would not be here.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Clause 13 is precisely the law as it is at present with the addition of the words I have cited, * of any international regulation,' making a violation of the international regulations when they are brought into force, a violation of the Act.

On section 14, penalty for violations.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The only change is the substitution of $1,000 for $100. The object in thus increasing the fine is that with some traps, particularly on the Pacific coast, it is possible for a trap owner to violate the law, and be fined $100, and still make money. The penalty was too small, and we are increasing it to $1,000 with that object especially in view.
Does this remove all other penalties that have been in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am advised it does not.
Does the minister think this fine of $1,000 will he sufficient to secure compliance with the law by the owners of traps?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The previous clause provides that all the property of a party violating the law may be confiscated. The $1,000 penalty is heavy, and it is deemed by the department to be sufficient. I do not think that owners of traps would violate the law very often if they were fined $1,000.
I would suggest in addition that the license of the man who violates the law should be cancelled, and a renewal refused.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is a question of policy. The department can very properly refuse a renewal to a habitual violater of the law.
In drafting a jaw with severe penalty, the cancellation of the license should be one of the penalties, so that a man would know what he was facing when he violated the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The law might be violated by a trap owner inadvertently, and it would be hardly proper to deprive him of a license when he was not guilty of intentional wrong-doing. However, as the power of renewal is absolutely in the hands of the department, it is believed that the interests of the government are sufficiently protected.

When the minister
reminds me of the fact that the discretion as to renewal lies absolutely in the hands of the department, and says that that should be a guarantee that the man would be punished, and the license not issued, I would recall some of our experiences on the inland lakes. Glaring violations of the law have been committed, and the officials in Selkirk and in the department here knew of it. An investigation was held costing this country $1,200, and after it had been demonstrated that the American fish interests were violating the
Mr. TEMPLEMAN
law, fishing twice the amount of nets allowed, fishing when they liked, and how they liked, the tools of the American Fish Company, for the company had no status in Canada, got their licenses year after year just the same. It is cases of this kind that make a man on this side anxious that the penalty should be included right in the Bill so that we we will be sure of its enforcement and not have to depend on the officials to protest Canadian interests.
On section 15, International fishery regulations may be brought into force.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: As the committee is aware, in the year 1908, a treaty was made between the United States and Canada, for the purpose of regulating the fisheries in the inland waters contiguous ito the two countries. By that treaty, commissioners were appointed by both governments under article 3, to prepare and put into operation with as little delay as possible, regulations, restrictions and prohibitions, with appropriate penalties for breaches thereof. The day when they were to come into operation was to be fixed by concurrent proclamation of the Governor General of Canada, and of the President of the United States. In pursuance of that article of the treaty, representatives of the United States and of Canada have agreed to regulations governing fishing in international waters as set out in the treaty. The clause in this Bill is to give to the Governor in Council power to bring those regulations into force by proclamation as required by the treaty. The proclamation in Canada and the proclamation in the United States are to toe issued concurrently. That is the only object of this clause. When the United States are ready to bring the regulations into force on their side of the line we want to ' be ready to proclaim the regulations on our side, and we have been advised by the Justice Department, that it is necessary that we should take this power by statute.

I would like to point out to the minister that while the penalty of $1,000 prescribed to this section, like the section we have just passed, may be sufficient on the Canadian side, there is grave reason to doubt whether it will be a deterrent on the American side. There has been a law on the American side against fishing traps in certain days of the week. The government knows from observation made last year that that law has not been carried out, and although there has been a suggestion that the authority for regulation and supervision shall be taken from the state and conferred upon and exercised by the federal jurisdiction, we have heard nothing of any progress made in that direction: and we have no assurance, so far as I have heard, that the federal government of the United States is to be in effective

control of the waters of the state of Washington. I presume if any such arrangement had been made it would have been communicated to the House by the minister just now. In the absence of any assurance of that kind, we are interested in what happened last year, and on that point I have the authority of Prof. David Starr Jordan, the American representative on the International Fisheries Commission. In his report to Washington he says:
With upwards of 2,5r0 square miles of fishing territory, the state of Washington has' no patrol vessels, and so far as I know, but a single gasoline launch. The present statutes are fairly well enforced in most of the eastern boundary states, notably so in Ohio and Pennsylvania. In Washington they are not adequately enforced. It is claimed that in the current season the fishermen of Washington caught by encroachment on the close season salmon to the value of upwards of $600,000 to which they were not entitled. Part of these should hare been taken in British Columbia waters. The others should have escaped up the Fraser river to the spawning grounds. In Canada, throughout the boundary waters, the statutes now in effect are rigidly enforced. It does not even occur to any one to violate them. The real need of the boundary situation is less that of stringent legislation than of equal enforcement of law on either side. I see no way to accomplish this except by a federal patrol, corresponding to the Dominion patrol of Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, if the only deterrent we have against the prospect of another American raid upon our salmon during the close season, a raid which netted $600,000 last year, is this fine of $1,000, which is the limit allowed by the international regulations, I fear it will be found ineffectual. I would like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that one of these traps caught last year as high as 110,000 fish in one day. At the price at which these fish were sold, 20 cents each, that would mean $22,000 worth of fish that one of these traps has been known to catch in a single day, and the sole penalty for an open and wilful violation of the law that will yield $22,-00U in one day would be a fine of $1,000. Of course any trap owner who could reap that rich harvest would accept the risk of a fine every time. I uould suggest to the minister that if there are to be any further negotiations in connection with the international regulations, he should press for some such further provision with respect to traps as he has now with respect to net fishing, that is, that if a net fisherman wilfully violates the law and the department ha.s cause of complaint against him as an incorrigible, the department may confiscate his license and his nets, and I would recommend that he press for power to deal in the same way with the trap fishermen. I would ask the minister whether the government has examined that phase
of the situation, and whether, in view of the enormous profits of trap owners to be obtained by paying a fine for violating 'the law, the government has considered it advisable to make the penalty more drastic than it is in these regulations.

I would be very glad if the government could see its way clear to suspend the clause of this Bill that relates to the confirmation of the international regulations with the United States. It seems to me that the regulations which have been framed, have not been framed with proper inquiry and proper care for the interest of the fishermen who have been carrying on operations in international waters. Along the whole length of the Detroit river men have been fishing for their life time; they have got their plants, and now, by the operation of this treaty and of these regulations, their business is going to be cut away from them. It may be that it is in the interest of fish culture generally that that should be done, but I think it would be much more satisfactory if a committee of this House could hear the fishermen themselves in order to find out whether the interest of the fishery is so very important as to require so drastic a measure as is proposed by these regulations. It appears to me that it has gone too far now. What I would like to suggest to the minister is that the matter be taken up with a view of a further conference in order to have it dealt with in the light of the greater information that can be got by hearing the fishermen themselves. They feel very much aggrieved. Many of them have almost made their living from fishing in the Detroit river. It is not so on the American side. There the river front is so much taken up with wharfs that they have not the fisheries on their side, and I can quite understand their acquiescence in regulations which are no loss to them. But on the Canadian side, where people have been fishing for their lifetime, or for many years, it is a great hardship, and I hope the minister will take this into consideration and see even at this hour if there is not some way of at least giving the fishermen a hearing.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I would point out to my hon. friend (Mr. A. H. Clarke) that the clause now before the House does not necessarily mean that the regulations agreed to are going to be proclaimed. I suppose that the government could refuse to proclaim them. They are simply taking power to bring these regulations into force. My attention has been called to the fact that one of the regulations affecting the fishing in boundary waters prohibits net fishing in the St. Mary's, St. Clair, Detroit, Niagara and St. Lawrence rivers where they form part of

the international boundary line. I am not in a position to say whether it would >be deemed advisable to prohibit net fishing altogether, but I would naturally suppose that net fishing in these waters was destroying the fish and it was deemed wise to prohibit net fishing. However, that is simply an expression of opinion. We 'take power to bring into force by proclamation any agreement that may be reached, [DOT]whether this agreement or a subsequent agreement is necessary, and it is necessary for the government to have that power, because otherwise no treaty made with the United States could be proclaimed and tnade law. I would suggest to my hon. friend that, while he may have a good 'point in trying to have that regulation changed, it does not necessarily follow 'that fishing in that way would be prohibited as a result of taking power to proclaim the treaty. Under the treaty the regulations are revisable by the mutual consent, I think, of both governments at 'any time, and it might be found that before the treaty was proclaimed, with the concurrence of the United States com-fnissioner^ a change in the treaty would 'be advisable. The treaty provides that it Shall remain in force for a four year 'period. In regard to my hon. friend from 'British Columbia (Mr. J. D. Taylor), I Vant to point out that the condition there *will be, in my opinion, vastly improved 'by this treaty. I think my hon. friend from New Westminster will admit that fact. Generally speaking hitherto there has been practically no law. well observed, at all events, in the state of Washington. The states control the fisheries, 'and up to the present time the state of Washington has had certain regulations, but these regulations were never enforced. 'A close season was not observed and our fishermen have thought that by the rather rigid enforcement of the regulations made by the Fisheries Department they were unfairly discriminated against. This treaty applies to the United States side of the line, with respect to the Pacific ocean, practically the regulations which hitherto 'have been in force in Canadian waters. The American government have undertaken to enforce these regulations, not the 'Washington state government. The United *States government take the ground. I think, upon the advice of their highest 'legal authority, that although the various fisheries are controlled and regulated by the states, when the federal government 'enters into a treaty with a foreign nowpr the right of the United States to regulate the fisheries is paramount and must prevail. Therefore, we feel quite sure that when the United States government undertake, in the words of the treaty, by legislation and executive action, the regulation and restriction of the fisheries we must denend unon them to carry out Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
their treaty obligations. The treaty does not impose any penalty; it simply provides that each government shall impose its own penalty for any infraction of the treaty. This government is imposing a penalty of $1,000 for a violation of the regulations under this treaty. I would assume that the United States government would impose about the same penalty. I quite agree with -what my hon. friend says with regard to the destructive character of the fishing carried on south of the boundary line. As a matter of fact, if we did not have this treaty with the United States government to regulate fishing in Puget Sound, and if no restriction, other than those which have been imposed in the past, were to be imposed in the future, we; might just as well conclude that fishing on the Fraser river, would be absolutely destroyed in another ten years. I read in a newspaper the other day a statement by the fishery inspector for British Columbia who, disheartened by the fact that thq people in the state, of Washington were not living up to their own regulations, and were catching -salmon which would, if not intercepted, have gone up the Fraser river to be caught by the Canadian fishermen, declared that if the United States would not impose effective restrictions, the restrictions imposed by the Canadian government should be removed, and apparently concluded that the river should be fished until the last fish was taken out of it. I do not think it is in the interests of the Canadian fishermen that this government should not make a very earnest effort indeed to obtain from the United States government a treaty imposing upon the citizens of that country the same restrictions as we are imposing upon the fishermen in British Columbia with the view to conserving the the great fishery of the Fraser river. I believe that this is a good treaty. As I un-i derstand its application to the province of British Columbia, I think it is a goodf treaty. I must confess with regard to other portions of Canada, and especially in regard to the complaint made by my hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. Clarke) I am not very familiar with the facts, but in regard to British Columbia, if we are ever going to restore the Fraser river to its position as a sock-eye stream we must do it by a treaty with the United States government. It is a fair treaty. The same regulations are to apply on each side of the boundary line. I know it is said that they will not carry them out. There is some little reason for that suspicion from lations were supposed to be carried out their regulations in the past, but the regulations were supposed to be carried out. by the state governments. Now, the obligation to do so is imposed upon the federal government, and I believe

that it is really in the interest of the fishermen of the Fraser river, in which interest the hon. member for New Westminster is speaking, more than in the interest of the canners, as well as in the business interests of British Columbia, that the yield of fish should be restored to its normal condition, as it can be by the enforcement of a treaty of this kind. Whether the American government will enforce the treaty as the Canadian government will enforce it I do not know, but I have faith enough in the American government to believe it will. At all events, if the treaty does not work well, we can terminate it in four years after it goes into effect, or try to get a better one.

I agree to a large extent with the remarks made by the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Clarke), and I believe to a great extent the Canadian fishermen have not had the opportunity they desire to present their case. I understand from the minister that while this Bill may pass it does not follow that it will come into force except by proclamation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The Bill will come into force when passed, but the clause under consideration takes power to proclaim the regulations concurrently with their proclamation in the United States.
It does not come into force automatically through the passing of the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No.
Would the fishermen of Canada have an opportunity of being heard as to the hardship these regulations may work upon them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The joint commission appointed by Canada and the United States to carry out the treaty can at any time hear the fishermen, and they have the power to revise or change any of the regulations.

It so happens that along the north shore of the Georgian bay, the north shore of Lake Huron, and Lake Superior, Rainy lake and the Lake of the Woods, the open lake is on the American side while the most of the islands are on the Canadian side, and this territory affords the best fishing grounds. In certain cases this Bill would not bear so hard on the fishing interests of the United States as on Canada from the minister's statement, I assume our fishermen will have a right to be heard before that joint commission which it is assumed will deal fairly with all these matters. If our fishermen have the right to present their case, and seek redress, notwithstanding the passage of the Bill, I would not so strongly object to it, but otherwise I would agree with the member for Essex that it would be better to defer this legislation.	'	[DOT]

I have given considerable attention to our fresh water fish supply, and I can say that in my opinion this legislation is an effort in the right direction. I believe that if the provisions of this treaty are carried out by the Americansy as it will be by the Canadians, honestly and faithfully, it is bound to have a good effect. The trouble in the past has been, and I suppose it will continue in the future, is to get the American officials to be honest in enforcing the law. I think we can depend on our officials to carry out faithfully their part of the duty cast upon them by the treaty. However, I want to point out to the member for Rainy River, as he no doubt knows, that on the Rainy lake for instance, nearly all the fishermen who have been engaged there, and on the Lake of the Woods have been fishing for American companies. The Canadian fisheries have been exploited for many years by large American concerns, and while the treaty makes it obligatory upon the Canadian government to protect their side of the line it does not deal with the Americans on the other side. I do not believe that Canadians would suffer so much loss as the Americans, for the reason, that two-thirds of the Canadian fishermen catching white fish, pickerel, and other species, on our lakes are largely in the employ of the American companies. It is an open secret that our laws have been openly violated for years on the Great Lakes, and the inland waters as well, by the American companies who have obtained control of our fisheries in a round about way. They get Canadians to take out licenses, and thus evade the law. We, on our part have not been receiving the benefit we should receive from our fish wealth. Lake Winnipeg used to be one of the greatest white fish fisheries in the world, but now it has been destroyed or nearly destroyed, simply because the Americans have been allowed to come into our waters, and evade our laws. They formed what they called the Dominion Fish Company which has operated all the way from Lake Winnipeg down to the great lakes and that fishing company was no other than the Booth Fishing and Packing Company of Chicago. I repeat that if the treaty is carried out faithfully it will have a beneficial effect, and I trust the minister will watch carefully to see that the Americans are not allowed to take advantage of us, but are compelled to live up to the terms of the treaty. The minister will have to watch them very closely in that respect. Now, the sturgeon fishery is a most important industry to us, and I notice that in the regulations under the treaty the commissioners

I am very glad to see my hon. friend from Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) and mv hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. Clarke) taking a hand in this discussion of fishery matters, especially on the side of the fishermen. The Bill under discussion is certainly an important one, especially as we are legalizing regulations that have been adopted by the joint commission. One thing in connection with these regulations which I cannot understand is that the north channel of the Georgian bay is included in the international waters, that is to say, the channel north of the Manitoulin island, which is many miles away from the United States, and is virtually a huge inland river or canal. The question of our fisheries being controlled by Americans is not at all a question of surmise. It is a fact that is established by the evidence of Prof. Prince given last year before a committee of this House. He stated that the boats and the gear used in the fishing business on the Great Lakes and on Lake Winnipeg were owned by Americans; and under a clause of their customs regulations fish caught in boats or with gear owned by Americans are admitted into the United States free of duty. The result of that has been, to place the fisheries of the Great Lakes entirely in the hands of Americans and to make Canadians virtually hewers of wood and drawers of water to the American companies. The fish taken from our inland waters by these companies is carried to the United States and put in cold storage, and when Canadians want any fish, it is sent back into Canada from Buffalo, Chicago and Sault Ste. Marie. It would not be difficult to correct this, but there is no use of mv asking the minister to make any change, because I know that it would not be made. The only thing to do would be to put a clause in the Act providing that foreign craft and gear would not be allowed to be used in Canadian waters. I think we have attained that measure of nationality where we should not any longer be hewers of wood and drawers of water to any people. The statements I have made are facts which cannot be controverted, as any one can see by looking at the evidence given last session by Prof. Prince before the committee on Marine and Fisheries.

It is quite true that the fishing interests of the Great Lakes are entirely in the hands of Americans. There is only one section, that is, the north shore

of Lake Superior, consisting of a stretch of 150 or 200 miles, where the fishermen own their own outfits and carry on the fishing on their own behalf. All the other fishing interests, on both the Canadian and the American side, are under the control of one or two companies. But I think my hon. friend's information is not correct when he says that American craft and American implements are used entirely in the taking of fish. What happens is that these American companies have gradually driven the Canadian fishermen into the position of catching fish for them, and later they have acquired their outfits, their tugs, their fishing smacks and their entire plant; so that, speaking generally, the Canadian fishermen are catching fish with the plants of these great companies, but they are Canadian bottoms. The trouble is not altogether with the licenses. The licenses are issued to Canadians, but the Canadians are in the service of these companies. The provincial government, I am speaking of the government of Ontario, for I know the circumstances perfectly well, are aware of this monopoly, and they have not yet adopted or grappled with 'anything in the shape of a remedy. Now, I do not know to what extent that could be remedied by action here, because this government does not give licenses for the taking of fish. It seems to me that the remedy could be used with much greater force by the provincial authorities than under the regulations of the federal authorities so far as Ontario is concerned. As I understand it, Ontario is the only province that has taken over the management and control of their own fisheries. The other provinces under some arrangement permit the federal authorities to issue licenses and to regulate the whole procedure of taking fish in the provincial waters. That is not the case in Ontario. Ontario has a department which manages and controls the whole matter. I am finding no fault at all. I am just pointing out that it is not so much a question of issuing licenses; it is the difficulty of finding a market, and that is where this American monopoly and the advantage and control, having the capital at their command. Whether there is anything in this treaty that will enable the joint commission to remedy an evil of that kind, I am not prepared to say. I doubt very much that there is such a remedy. Speaking of Ontario, I am afraid it will not be remedied unless the provincial government takes very strong action in the matter, or unless there is some arrangement made by which this government would assume control and make regulations necessary to put an end to that monopoly.

What the hon. gentle^ man said suggests another question on
which I had intended to say something, and that is the question of the American fish interests in the west. Now, the hon. gentleman says that the Americans do not' own the nets and gear and boats. I want to say most emphatically that the American fish companies on Lake Winnipeg have owned for years every steamboat, every sail boat and all the nets that were used in that lake by those companies up to a year or two ago. They secured the license in defiance of the law. The law is pretty clear and well defined that no license should be issued except to a British subject, and that that subject should own all his boats and gear. That is laid down in the fisheries regulations, as drastic a law as there is on the statute-book. But that law has been evaded openly and the Fisheries Department has been aware of it for years. There has been no secret about it at all.
Whose fault is it?

The fault must lie with the officials or with the department, because it has been an open secret and everybody knew about it. It has been going on for the list fifteen or eighteen years now. How does it operate? There is a duty on all fresh fish that goes into the United States, but under some 'special arrangement with the 'Customs Department of the United States any fish said to have been taken in gear owned by American citizens is admitted free. The consequence is that in Lake Winnipeg the American companies, taking the oath that the fish were caught in their own nets, get the fish into the United StateS free, while the fish taken by Canadian fishermen in Canadian nets has to pay three-quarters of a cent duty on the fish. I say that is a great hardship, and the government should take very drastic measures to compel the enforcement of the law so that Americans will not be able to control our waters to the detriment of our Canadian fishermen. The Booth Fi3h Packing Company^ failed in Chicago about a year ago, I think. Now, what happened? The great plant of the Dominion Fish Company came under the hammer, and there was proof positive that that great company owned that plant. As soon as it failed in Chicago everything belonging to it was tied up. I repeat it is an open secret, and something in regard to which the goverment ought to take action. To say that the American fish companies do not control our waters is a great mistake. The American fish companies have controlled them for years, and it is up to the Fishery Department to take the full responsibility. This matter has been brought before them time after time, and surely there must be some way by which the gov* ernment could protect their own waters,

especially the inland waters. There is no. reason under the sun why the American companies should come to Lake Winnipeg and be allowed to control that lake to the detriment of our own fishermen. That has been going on for fifteen years, and as the licenses are issued by the Dominion gov-erment, it is a matter absolutely undeT the control of this government which ought to act in defence of our fisheries.

I may say that
under the international regulations the government takes control of the gear. They limit the number and size of the nets that shall be allowed and various other things, so that I think the jurisdiction over the gear is certainly in the Dominion government. The licenses, as we have seen in Manitoba, are issued by the Dominion government, and they permit this work to go on in Manitoba. It is quite true that licenses to fish without virtually any control are issued by the Ontario government, but the only control the Ontario government ha3 is in Georgian bay, and a large section of that control has been taken away by these very regulations, because it puts the North channel, one of the best fishing grounds, under international waters. I think the government should take action in this matter, and that something should be done which would gradually return the control and operation of our fisheries to the hands of Canadians and Canadian capital.

All I have to sav in connection with this Bill, and clause lfi, is that the minister should not be in too great a haste to bring the regulations into force. I think it is highly desirable that plenty of time should be taken. I know that in the western part of Lake Ontario the fishermen will be obliged to procure new nets under the new regulations, because they will be compelled to fish with a net of a different mesh when these regulations are brought into force. Now, these men are anxious not to be forced to do that too soon, and they desire to be permitted to use their own nets practically until they are worn out. Instead of the regulations being brought into force at the end of the year 1910, I think the time should be postponed for at least another year. By that time the nets now in use would be pretty well worn out and the fishermen would be ' obliged to secure new nets in any event.
therefore, appeal to the bon. minister in the hope that he will exercise his influence with the other members of the government, and not have these regulations brought into force too hurriedly. There may be a way out of some of the difficulties that have been referred to by hon. gentlemen tonight. Perhaps some new investigation may be made by the two countries, and I

hope that better counsels will prevail, and that so far as the part of the country I live in is concerned there will be no interference, at any rate for another year, by which time the fishermen will be better prepared to enter upon the changed conditions.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed.
House in committee on Bill (No. 163) to amend the Volunteer Bounty Act of 1908.- Mr. Oliver.

When this matter was up before I asked the minister whether or not the government had given any intimation to the public last year as to any possible changes. His reply was ' not in his recollection '. My memory happened to be better than his and I said so. I wish now to bring to his attention his reply on February 4 of last year to a question by my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe). The question was
Has the government Under consideration any change in the conditions relating to the South African land grants.
The minister's reply was:
No changes are contemplated.
That was the reply to a question which . covered absolutely this condition as to the time. A minister coming here ought to be up in the subject to be discussed, and should not make statements such as he made to me on that occasion which are absolutely misleading. I object entirely, or almost entirely to any change in those conditions because the great majority of that scrip has got into the hands of speculators, it is out of the hands of the men who actually earned it, and if a special bonus of this kind is to be given by the government it should be given to the men who went out and took their lives in their hands. I would not object to this additional time being given in the case of military bounty warrants still held by the volunteers, or by the widows or heirs of men who died in the service. The government should also consider the case of those who went out there, such as nurses who took care of our boys in time of sickness, but who were not under military supervision, and for that reason did not get warrants. Their case ought to be taken up, and a recognition of their services in this way would meet with little, if any, opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend has seen fit to open his remarks by the suggestion that I was not frank to the House in a statement I made last session. If my memory and understanding are right, the

question at issue and under consideration at that time was the extending of the scope of the Act, and I replied at that time as I reply now, and as this Bill is the evidence, that the government had no intention of changing the Act. The extension of time for the location is not a change in the principle of the Act, but a change in the operation of the Act, and that matter is now submitted to this parliament for their judgment. If it is in accordance with the judgment of parliament this extension will be given, if it is not it will not be given. As to extending the operation of the Act to embrace other classes, it was the judgment of parliament in 1908 that the Act should apply to the people to whom it was made to apply. The government has seen no reason to change the opinion then expressed. That is to say it has seen no reason that would warrant the opening of the Act, and the widening of its scope as has been suggested on various occasions. Therefore on this occasion the government offers for the consideration of the House the proposition that the. time for the location of the warrants granted under this Act shall be extended for one year, being moved to do so by the request of the men who were themselves volunteers and who by reason of their election to the position had the right to speak for the volunteers who went to South Africa, and were entitled to this scrip.
Has the minister any idea how many of these warrants are still in the hands of the original holders?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no means of knowing that. There have been issued altogether 6,846 warrants, and of these 3,142 have been either located or the transfer has been registered. There remain 3,704, or more than one-half which have not been accounted for, and of the present possession of which we have no knowledge. So far as we know they are still in the hands of the parties to whom they were issued.
Was the scrip for lands given in years gone by under similar circumstances negotiable?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, yes.
In every case?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.

And in all former scrips of this kind the time for location was extended for many years, year after year. I have to leave in one-half hour and will not be here again this week, so that I may not have another opportunity of discussing the Bill, and if you will allow me I would like to discuss it now for a few minutes. 1 hava an amendment to section 4, and this will probably be my sole opportunity of 256
discussing it. It is not for the purpose of extending the scope of the Bill. The amendment is to cover the case of those veterans, or the substitutes, the assignees of the veterans, who have located their scrips on different half-sections throughout the country, some of whom, a small proportion, have unfortunately been either misled by others or have misled themselves, and have located their warrants on land that subsequently turns out to be practically worthless. They are in this position, that it will not pay them to go on and put in their three years residence on that half section in order to secure the patent, and under the present Act it seems the minister has no authority, or claims to have no authority, to allow them to make an exchange. Now, here is the way it has worked out. Take the case of one young man in my constituency, a man who has been in that country for 15 or 20 years. He volunteered to go to the war, he went all through the war, and he got his warrant. He went away southwest of Moosejaw, 150 or 200 miles, he spent over $100 in cash looking at various lands, and he selected five or six different half-sections. He came back to the office at Moosejaw. In the meantime it had been advertised that some half dozen or dozen townships were to be opened on a certain day, townships he had looked at. When he got back to Moosejaw, there was a tremendous rush for the land. He had to get in line with the others, he was some 40 or 50 back from the head of the line, and by the time he got to the counter every one of the sections that he had examined personally, and of which he had selected three, had all been taken. When he got there the man in front of him said to him: There, I got my first choice. But there is another section that is first-class, just as good as the one I took. Now, this man wanted to avoid what might easily happen a second time, he did not want to be obliged to spend another $150 in cash to go back and make a second selection, and here was a chance to get a first-class section. The Tesult was that he took the man's advice, and he made an entry there and then for a homestead preemption, and also located his warrant that he had earned himself as a volunteer in South Africa on the other half-section. Then he immediately goes back to this land and examines it, and he finds that the man who gave him the information was either deceived himself, or had deliberately deceived the man of whom I am speaking, Mr. Brockway, one of my constituents, and he found out that both the section of land entered for homestead and pre-emption and the other section under warrant were absolutely worthless. He told me he could not get $10 for the section. Now, the department allows him to abandon his home-



stead pre-emption and take up another on payment of $10 for 'the entry. But, so far as the warrant is concerned he cannot do that. He. >is therefore in the position of losing one or the other of them, and all I am asking is that an amendment be made to the law-I do not think myself that it needs an amendment, I think the minister has the authority, but he thinks not, and his opinion goes-but if an amendment is necessary I think there should be one made to that clause that would permit a man who has selected a half-section under a warrant and who finds the land is no* good, to enable that man for once-I would only give him one more chance-to abandon that and get authority to substitute another half-section under the same warrant. Now, I have mentioned one case, but I have another case that is ten times more serious. There are a number of oases of hardship, but this one is an especially glaring case, and I want to bring it to the attention of the committee to show how unfairly this law may work out. It is the case of a man who formerly lived in my constituency, his brother is at present in my constituency. This man himself has moved up west of Batitleford and located land there. I will read a copy of his letter:
Stainsleigh, Alberta, Nor-ember 5, 1909.

Turriff, M.P..
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Turriff,-I had the pleasure of meeting you once many years ago when I was teaching at Carnduff; my brother, J. A. Thompson was Massey-Harris agent at C., and you were agent for that company at Estevan. Not on the grounds of that slight acquaintance, hut because you are familiar with our western conditions, and because I believe you have a sympathy with a thing .that is essentially just, I am making free to ask your assistance in a matter of very great importance.
I have been unable to do a day's work since midsummer of 1905, when I was stricken down with tuberculosis of the spine. Dr. Chown. of Winnipeg, diagnosed my disease, and I have for past four years been under the treatment of Dr. Clarence L. Starr, an ortho-poedic specialist of Toronto.
In 1906 I came west to homestead, locating on N.E. 18-T. 40-R. 1-W. 4. I have resided on my homestead continually since May 5, 190S, sleeping under canvas from that date until the present, excepting two and a half months the hitter winter of 1906-7.
Last winter I purchased two South African scrip claims, believing that by doing the necessary duties to prove up on the land I saw means of making provision for my wife, my children and myself. In this way I would be making use of practically the only earning power I possessed.
I may say that this man was a minister, either a Presbyterian or a Methodist, when he was stricken down with this disease.

In the purchase of the scrip I invested about all that I owned, as it seemed to me a perfectly safe venture. It was utterly impossible for me to endure the driving necessary to locate land myself, and I had to depend on some one else to do the work for me. I had arrangements made with a conple of men who were thoroughly competent and reliable to make an exploring tour for me, when a conple of men -with whom I had an intimate acquaintance, came to me with the story that they had unexpectedly made a discovery of some excellent land and, knowing my wish to locate land, had hurried across to give me the first chance. The land was within seven miles of a town; peculiar circumstances had prevented it being filed in before, and if I wanted the land I must decide immediately, and get out at once to secure it, as land-suckers rvere in all around, and such land as this would soon be picked up. I trusted them without the slightest misgiving, and, being unable to examine the land personally, and supposing they were really showing me some consideration because of my position, I hurried to Battleford and filed the land. I filed on May 5.
