The land proved to be worthless. Three-quarters are absolutely worthless for either agricultnre or pasture, and the fourth quarter has fair surface, but is underlaid with gravel. To spend the money necessary to do the duties would be to make an outlay for which there would he no compensating return.
I paid $50 for the locator's information, and they took the entire responsibility. It was pure fraud on their part.
The land on which I filed is S.E. 18 and 8. i-7 in Tp. 38, R. 28, W. 3rd M. Homestead Inspector McArthur, inspector for that district, chauced to call on me, and, at my request made an examination of my land. His report was forwarded by R. E. A. Leech, inspector of agencies to the department with riequest that, owing to special conditions, some consideration be shown. The deputy minister replied stating that the law did not allow the privilege of abandonment with a view to re-entry.
So this disposition of the question means almost complete financial ruin to me, and involves an essential injustice, I am wishing to ask for a consideration of the question by the minister, or if the minister feels that he should not exercise discretionary power owing to the wording of the law, should not a law that involves such hards rips aud injustice he changed.	,
Dr. Clark is member for our constituency and will, I feel sure, lead in advocacy of my cause. John Tolmie, of Kincardine, Ontario, has promised to support earnestly any effort made to secure redress for me. If you feel that my request is right when I seek redress, may I not ask for the kindness of your support. Your familiarity with homestead conditions will make your advocacy of special value to me.
Trusting that you may feel free to grant me the favour that I ask, I am,
Sincerely yours,

There is a case surely that would call for the sympathy of any member of this House. This man has already been to

blame in the matter, but under the law he cannot get any redress, and what I ask is that section 4 be amended as follows:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask the hon. gentleman, if he is proposing to enter into a discussion of section 4 or to offer an amendment, to wait until we come to that section.

I am quite aware that I am transgressing the rules of the House, but I have to leave in a few minutes, and with the permission of the House I would offer this amendment:
That section i of the Volunteer Act, 1908, chapter 66, be amended by adding to it the following words: ' Every such grantee or his substitute may within six months after the date of entry, abandon the land so entered and may thereafter, within the time limited for selection and entry by subsection 1 of this section, or within six months after such date, make a second entry; provided that nothing in this subsection shall authorize or entitle any grantee or his substitute to make any further entry in place of the land abandoned as aforesaid.'
That is to say that he shall have the opportunity of making one exchange, but no more. It is probable that out of 6,000 or 7,000 cases, there will not be more than a hundred cases in which such an exchange is made. It seems to me a small matter to do that. We have taken the position that it is proper and right to give a South African veteran a half-section of land, and that being the case he should be given the opportunity of making an exchange if he has got poor land. We all know that when a man takes up a homestead he can abandon that homestead or it may be cancelled. He may enter for ten homesteads and have them all cancelled, and if he does so he does not lose his homestead right. In that case we are giving the land for nothing. Here is the case of the South African veteran who has served in the war in South Africa for the empire, or, in the case of the substitute, here is the man who has bought his warrant at a price ranging all the way from $300 to $1,000. I think it is only fair and just that some consideration should be given to these men. This is the amendment that I wish to make to subsection 4, and I trust that you will see that it is passed.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if that amendment would not have the effect of extending the operation of the Act for six months beyond the year for which it has already been extended?

No, it would extend the time for six months only to make the ex-256i
change, but it would not extend the time for the location of the warrant.
It would have the effect of extending it for six months under the Act.

In spite of the explanation given by the minister as to what he meant, the words I read were absolutely plain. In answer to the question:
Has the government under consideration any change in the conditions relating to South African land grants?
His answer was:
No changes are contemplated.
The point I want to make is that if he did not understand the meaning of the question, the hon. member for Lisgar had in mind nothing else except the possibility of an extension of the time. The people who held the warrants believed that the minister's answer meant that by the end of 1910 the time for taking up these warrants would expire. For that reason, many of them sacrificed those warrants for a very inconsiderable price as compared with their actual value-somewhere about $700 and down to $500. They sacrificed their claims because they believed that the Minister of the Interior meant what he said in answer to the hon. member for Lisgar. There is no question that that was the belief of the majority of the people in Canada. Even the men who were buying and dealing in scrip, in making a deal, brought in an argument in favour of low prices that by the end of 1910 the warrants would be of no use whatever, and they could not resell them. For that reason they acted as bears on the market and held down the price. That was the case until January of this year when we find that a firm who dealt in half-breed scrip before and are now dealing in bounty warrant scrip came down here and had an interview with the minister, or some official, or some one who was in the know. They telegraphed to their brokers in Winnipeg to buy all the scrip they could get. That is a true sign that there was inside information given to men who were dealing in scrip with the view of putting up the value of the warrants. For that reason I think we should have an explanation from the minister before he forces this legislation through. In the west it has been generally understood that in matters appertaining to the west the minister's word is good, and a year ago he gave his word absolutely in this connection. I would feel hurt personally if on this occasion he departed from the course bv which he has won this good name.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know that there is any use of my hon. friend and myself imputing motives across the floor of the

House. My hon. friend has seen fit to represent that I did not give a frank answer to a question that was asked, last year, and he tells the House now what was in the mind of the questioner when he asked the question, and what was in the mind of the House when the question was asked. The only question that had been under consideration was as to whether there should be other rights included in the grant. There was no question of an extension of time and whatever may have been in the mind of the questioner or whatever may have been in the mind of the House I may be permitted to answer that what was in my mind, and what my answer was given in regard to the question of the extension of the provisions of the Bill and not in regard to the question of the extension of time. However, from that my hon. friend has seen fit to say that I gave a pledge or a promise that there would be no legislation. My hon. friend has not read any such words from 'Hansard'. He has not read any words that could be construed into that meaning.	What I said was
that the government had not in contemplation a change in the Act. So that whether the hearer thought I meant one thing or meant another, there was no pledge on my part or on the part of the government. I stated the fact whether you take the one meaning or the other: that the government had not in contemplation. But, as my hon. friend is aware, there have been representations made to the government since last session upon this subject, representations that were entitled to some weight, representations made by the official representatives of the volunteers, asking specifically for an extension of time for location for a period of two years. The government did not think it well to accede to the request for a two years' extension, but thought that a one year's extension would not be any serious injury to the public interest and would remove any complaint that might seriously be made against the short time that was given for the location of the scrip. It was with the desire, and only with the desire to do what was fair and right by the people to whom the bounty was extended, and to do no more than was fair and right, so that there should not be any undue advantage to any particular class of the community nor any undue disadvantage to the settlement of the western country. Since the matter was up in the House before, I have received this copy of a circular on the subject, which I will take the liberty to read:-
Committee.-Capt. W. Hart McHarg, Vancouver, British Columbia ; Lt.-Col. W. G. Hurdman, Ottawa, Ontario; Col. G. Sterling Ryerson, M.D., Toronto, Ontario ; Major H. B. Stairs, D.S.O., Halifax, Nova Scotia; Major F. C. Jamieson, Strathcona, Alberta;

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
Macdonald, D.S.O., Winnipeg, Manitoba; Major B. R. Armstrong, St. John, New Brunswick; Major W. A. Weeks, Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island; Lt.-Col. 0. C. C. Pelletier, Quebec, Quebec; Major J. Cooper Mason, D.S.O., Toronto, Ontario; Lt.-Col. Wm. Hamilton Merritt, Toronto, Ontario, Secretary.
Toronto, Ontario, April 18, 1910.
Dear Sir,-We have read the discussions which took place in the House in connection with Mr. Oliver's Bill to extend the time by one year in which the South African veterans may locate their grants. It appears to be the wish of some of the members that those persons who have speculated in these warrants should secure none of the advantages which an extension of time would involve, and in so far as the advantages which should accrue to the veterans themselves are secured, this committee is desirous also that these speculators should be given no consideration.
The amendment Which has been suggested, however, we feel, will work to the disadvantage of both the veteran and the speculator, and in nullifying the advantages which the veteran would receive under the original Act, would destroy entirely the purpose of that Act.
If the extension is granted only to those persons who still retain their scrip on the understanding that these people will themselves locate their own land, the cash price will doubtless suffer, and those who have held in the hope of receiving full value for their grants will be forced to sell within the next nine months at such prices as they may be able to get, and as it is apparent at this time that two years was not a sufficient time for all this scrip to be absorbed without manipulations on the part of the speculator, it is likely that the prevailing price during the next nine months will show the result of the forced sale of a large number of grants within a short time.
On the other hand if the Bill grants the extension for all scrip at the present time in the hands of the original holders, who will be entitled to settle or sell as they may desire, it is felt that such legislation will have the effect of establishing two classes of scrip on which there will be a separate and distinct price, (a) Scrip that must be located within the present year, and (b) scrip that need not be located until the end of 19X1. This would doubtless serve the purpose intended, but we feel that the confusion arising therefrom would lower the prices of both classes of scrip and there would be many misunderstandings, and intending purchasers would be obliged to have scrip verified at Ottawa before it would be safe for them to purchase. In the United States scrip has depreciated in value on account of the doubtful authenticity of part of it and of the trouble involved in establishing the authenticity, and a similar condition would doubtless prevail in this country.
We think that in the interests of the veterans the Act should be passed in the form in which it was presented to the House. In asking for the extension we are not asking for more than we believe it was the government's intention we should have when the Act was

passed in 1908, sufficient time to allow of all this scrip being taken up or sold without unduly forcing or crowding the sale of it all in a shorter time than the natural supply and demand laws would take care of it.
Yours very truly,
WM. HAMILTON MERRITT, Lt.-Col.,
Secretary.
Is the hon. gentleman in accord with the position stated in that circular?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is not necessary for me to say whether I am in accord with it or not. I am presenting to the House a Bill which these gentlemen see fit to endorse. Their reasons for endorsing the Bill may not be the same as mine, for presenting, the Bill, but our conclusion is the same when we ask the House to support it.

'object, and I object a* strongly as I cau.
I do not see that the minister has made any case at all for this extension to the speculator. He says, in the language of the circular-and I understand that on a previous occasion he adopted much the same contention-that unless you grant it to the transferee, the present Holder of South African scrip will not get the benefit that the Act intends. That is to say, unless he is able to sell and is not forced to lo-'cate, he will be compelled to throw his *scrip on the market in the next few months j 'at whatever the market will stand. That imay be the case, but it is easily gotten 'over. If the minister does not propose to 'throw a plum to the speculator, why not say that only such scrip as is now in the hands of South African veterans shall be [DOT]entitled to the benefits of this Act? There was something in the circular venturing to argue that to do so would be an inconvenience to the soldiers, but so weak was it that the minister refused to endorse it. It argued that if you are going to draw a distinction between the scrip now in the hands of the veterans and that in the hands of speculators, you are going to compel the purchaser of scrip held by the Original grantee to make a search to make certain that it is so held, and that it is distinct from the scrip already transferred. That is not very much of a hardship. Here is a grantee who holds his scrip getting a material advantage over the one who has sold. He has not much to complain of if, in order to effect his sale, he has to *make a search at Ottawa. Surely the minister was well advised in declining to endorse the argument embodied in the end of the circular, which I will venture to say was framed by some astute solicitor acting not lor the veterans but for the speculators. T know nothing myself as to the composition of that circular. I simply judge how it arose by the way it reads and by the arguments therein contained. There is no difficulty whatever in limiting the benefit [DOT]of this amendment, if it is to go through -and apparently the minister is determined that it shall-to the veteran who has earned the scrip. Why should we grant that benefit to the speculator who has purchased, and who has secured his grant at a bargain by reason of the minister's words of the 4th of February last? This is certainly a grant of something that belongs to the Crown. The very extension is an increment of the value that is now a possession of the people of Canada, and, if this Act passes, that will go to the speculator. Why should the speculator get that for nothing? The principle is bad and cannot be defended, particularly in view of the fact that he bought on the understanding, so far as the vendor was concerned, that no such increment was to be Mr. MEIGHEN.
added. Therefore I submit that it is the duty of the minister to submit an amendment limiting the benefits oi this Act to such as at the time of the passing of this Act were the original grantees.

I am at a loss to understand what my hon. friend who has just sat down means when he talks about the people wdio bought scrip from the veterans as being speculators, in a tone implying that they are people who should be despised. The men who bought scrip from the South African veterans were gentlemen doing a service to the veterans who lived in eastern Canada.
I said nothing derogatory of the speculators.

If my hon. friend thinks that those whom he dubs speculators are perfectly estimable people and that no legislation should be passed to discriminate against them, then I do not understand what the whole tenor of his speech was about.
I do not want to discriminate against them; neither do I want 'to discriminate jin favour of them.
My hon. friend proposed an amendment which would be a discrimination against them.
Just leave them wdiere they are now.

Why should they not be treated as well as anybody else? I say that the speculator who bought the land from the veteran who lived in the east was a public benefactor. Those of us who sat in parliament and pressed on the minister and the government the wisdom of granting these lands to the men who went to South Africa did not want the boys who lived in our counties, when their rights to these lands accrued, to be,. compelled to go to the Northwest in order to get the benefit of them. We all hoped, we all knew, and we all expected that there was to be an opportunity to dispose of these rights once they were given to them, and I am sure a great many of us who were proud of our veterans would not have been so enthusiastic about the grant if we knew it meant to take away our boys to the west. We anticipated that their rights would be disposed of, and that there would be some people in this country who would want to buy them. There is no use in saying that those boys who went to South Africa and got the scrip did not know what they were doing. It is an imputation upon their intelligence and ability which is at least as good as that of ordinary citizens, it is, I say, an imputation upon their intelligence and ability to say that these boys * when they sold their scrip did not know

what they were doing, or that they, were not doing what they wanted to do, and that when somebody came along and gave them in cash what they did not want to take in kind, they were not entitled to take it. They did not want to leave their homes to go to the west: Now why should a man who gave a veteran the value for his scrip be treated differently from any one who buys real estate in this country? That is the proposition. There are to-day outstanding 3,704 warrants to men who went to South Africa that have not been located, and that have not been sold, and those veterans, those boys who went to South Africa want to sell them, and want to get the most they can out of them, and they have a perfect right to do that. But my hon. friend says the minister said last year that there was not going to be any extension of time. Probably there were some gentlemen who did not want to see any extension of time granted. There might not have been anything contemplated by the government, but I am in close touch with a large number of young men who are veterans, and I know that they looked forward and believed that the government this year would grant an extension in order that they would have more time to dispose of those warrants. They hoped it would be done, and they fully expected it would be done. I have had communications from some veterans who live in the east, and whose names are on the circular which was read by the minister, and I discussed the matter frequently with them during last year, and they hoped for an extension, and they believed it would come.
May I ask the hon. member a question. After the question was asked last year, how much did the value of the scrip depreciate on account of the answer?

My hon. friend was probably more interested in the value of the scrip than I was. I did not follow the fluctuating value of that scrip. But I may say for the benefit of my hon. friend that I have been pressing upon the minister for the past two years the desirability of this legislation in the interests of the men in the east who wanted to sell their scrip, pressing for an extension of the time in which location should be made so that the men who were late in taking out their warrants for various reasons, and every one knows there were a great many reasons why the taking out of those warrants was delayed, should have an op-jportunity of getting every dollalr they oould out of them. Speaking for the east, without any prejudice against our good friends in the west in whose future we all take a pride, I may say that we are specially jealous of the fact that our boys are going west. There are plenty of vigorous people going into that western country with the view of building it up, but we hope that our boys in the east will stay at home .and we want them to get all they can out of those warrants and give their vigour and energy to the eastern coun-1 try. Where more than half are not located up to date, are we going to limit them and prevent them from getting every dollar they can. I say that the man who buys this land from the veterans in the east is a benefactor to the veteran who wants to sell and who does not want to go out to the west, and there should be no discrimination at any time which would impair the value of the warrants given to the boys who went to South Africa and who are entitled to get every dollar out of those warrants possible.

It seems to me that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) rather misconceives the effect of the proposition. There is not, as I understand it, any desire to discriminate against the speculator, but we all heard the minister say that the motive that inspired this legislation was to protect the interests of the South African veterans and to enhance the benefit to be derived by them from their scrip. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) speaks with a good deal of indignation against any attempt to do anything that would in any way prevent the South African veterans from getting the full value for their scrip. Now, 1 am prepared to be as indignant as he is against any endeavour of that kind, but as I understand it the suggested amendment cannot in the slightest degree affect what any South African veteran has got or will get for his scrip. It will not affect what he has got, because the man who sold it has now got every dollar he is ever going to get, whether this legislation is passed or not, and it will not affect what any South African veteran will get in the future, because, as I understand1 it, the suggestion is to limit the application of this Act to scrip that is now held by South African veterans. Provided it is now held by a South African veteran, he will be at perfect liberty to sell it at any time after the passing of this Act, and will receive the enhanced value that will attach to it by reason of the extension of time.
Does not the hon. member recognize that the effect of the legislation is to discriminate against the man who is prepared to purchase scrip from the veteran?

The effect of this legislation is to confer a benefit on the South African veterans and to decline to give the same benefit to the man who is not a South

African veteran, but who is a member of a very respectable class, whom the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) describes as the purchasers of real estate. The hon. member asks why should this particular purchaser of real estate be treated differently from any other purchaser of real estate? I say he certainly should not be. But in what other instance has legislation been introduced to enhance the value of the property of the purchasers of real estate? Nobody ever came before this House and said that the purchasers of real estate are a deserving class in the community and therefore we will enact legislation to make their property more valuable than it was when they bought it. and yet that is precisely the position that will be created if this legislation is made applicable to scrip in the hands of persons who have bought and purpose re-selling it. These very excellent persons bought scrip which gave them a right to a property provided it was located before the 31st of January, 1910. With that restriction upon it that property had a value, and when they bought it, they presumably paid that value. However excellent people they may be, I do not think I am doing any injustice in saying they paid that value and not more than that value. What they bought and paid for they have got, they have everything they bought, a right to that property provided they located before the 31st of December, 1910.
Does that not also apply to veterans?

The veteran has today everything the legislation gives him; but this parliament says that we consider that the South Africa veteran is entitled to something further and we, out of our judgment that perhaps we did not give him as much as his services earned, are prepared to give him a little more, but we do that because we think under all the circumstances his services earned a little more. In the case of the purchaser, that man got precisely what he bought, and paid for, and we are coming in now by legislation to attach an additional value to that thing which the especially privileged purchaser of real estate bought. We are doing that out of consideration for the merits of the gentleman who sold to him, and that gentleman will not get one cent more. So we are going to reward this purchaser for having purchased from a very meritorious p/erson. The legislation as it stands makes a distinction or a discrimination between this particular kind of purchaser of real estate and all other kinds of purchasers of real estate. I ask in all fairness why this House should come to the rescue of a particular purchaser more than of any other pur-Mr. DOHERTY
chaser. The hon. gentleman says that the South African veteran when he sold knew what he was doing. I do not want to question that, but again we say that the purchaser when he bought knew what he was doing, and if he did not receive any increase he would have no ground on which to say that he was to have anything more than the right to this property provided he located it within this particular period of time. I have been seeking a reason why this gentleman should be given- this advantage. It is not a question of legislation to his detriment, it is a question of whether we shall legislate to confer an advantage on him. I had the advantage of receiving a copy of the circular which the hon. gentleman has read, I read it carefully, and I have listened to its reading by the minister. As far as that circular argues against any restriction that will bear on the scrip in the hands of the veterans, I have nothing to say. I am not arguing for anything that would affect that, but when the writer goes on to find reasons why this legislation should apply even to scrip that has already been sold, and is in the hands of a purchaser, then it seems to me that my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), has done ample justice to that reason. What does the reason consist of? That there Will be two classes ol scrip, and the man who goes to buy the scrip will therefore have to find out whether the scrip he is buying is of one class or the other. What does that difference reduce itself to? That the gentleman who goes to buy will have to verify the claim that the gentleman he buys from is a South African veteran, the original holder.
In a case where a young man, say in the east, has assigned, as I know he has done in two cases, to his brother who lived in the west
The amendment I suggested before would not exclude that brother. The purpose of the amendment I proposed is not to get at cases of that kind.
How would you help yourself?

I would provide that the extension would not cover cases of that kind. My amendment reads:
That section 4 be amended by inserting in the second line, after the word ' Act,' the following words:
Or any bounty certificate that has been, prior to the passage of this Act, sold or transferred to any person acquiring the same for purposes of speculation or resale.
When I suggested that it should be put in that shape, I did so, precisely to avoid injuring in any way, the person who would have acquired under circumstances, such

as have been, suggested, and I think there is a reason for making the difference. Where a South African veteran has parted with his scrip to any relative, where the consideration is presumably the affection of the veteran for the person to whom he chooses to give it, then in giving the enhanced value to the person to whom the veteran gave the land, you are indirectly benefiting him, you are giving to the person on whom he chooses to confer that benefit the benefit he would himself have got, and you are indirectly benefiting him. The situation is different from the situation with which I have been dealing. My amendment would cover the case of a man who went out into the market and bought with a view to resale. In the case of the latter man this legislation simply enhances the value of what he bought. In the case where the South African veteran has chosen to part with his scrip to a relative or a friend where it is not a matter of some one coming in and trying to turn the property over for a profit, where it is not being dealt with commercially, I would not make my amendment apply. I quite understand that in restricting it as I do, I am perhaps enabling some classes of persons, who ought not to get the benefit, to do so, but I want it made clear, that I am not desirous of doing anything that either directly or indirectly through others will injuriously affect the veteran. The case I would like to see excluded from the operation of the Act, is the case of the man who purchases to resell, the man who speculates in this scrip. I have no criticism to make of that man, but as I have said, I have not heard suggested one reason why this parliament should intervene to make that speculator's property more valuable, or his speculation more likely to be profitable. I do not see why we should give an advantage to that man more than to any other real estate speculator.
What tribunal is to try out the question of the intention that exists in the mind of the party who purchases as to whether he is going to sell or not?

Of course when the party comes forward to claim the right to make his location, he wdll have to produce his title. 1 call attention to the fact that the original purchaser under my amendment would not be precluded from locating. I am not trying to reduce the time of the man who has bought and actually located. Where I find the evidence of his purpose in making the purchases where you have to look for evidence is in what he does, that is to say, where you find the intention proved by the fact that the person who will come and locate will be a person who bought from a person
who had bought from the original holder; there you will have at all events a prima facie case that the original holder bought for the purpose of reselling. It may be susceptible of rebuttal, but my hon. friend knows that it is not at all an exceptional case that courts are called upon to decide what was the intention in doing a particular act. What people do speaks loudly as to what people intend to do. Now of course in the practical application of this, it would be for the department to take its position whether they will recognize the particular application or not, and if an application is refused and it is considered unjustly refused, why, the person holding the scrip will have his recourse to the court of competent jurisdiction.
My hon. friend does not indicate what tribunal has to determine this -question.

I did not rise for the purpose of giving to my hon. and learned friend a complete course in law, of which he has no need at my 'hand. But if I understand it rightly, the transferee of this scrip who would claim the right to locate a property and who would have that right refused to him because the time had expired, will be in the position of a man whose rights the Crown was_ refusing to recognize. Does my hon. friend think I am right to that extent?
. Mr. MACDONALD. You are getting along pretty well, but it is rather complicated.

Now in what does his position differ from the position of any man who has a claim against the Crown which the Crown disputes? As I understand the law, where a man has a claim against the Crown, and the Crown disputes it, he is entitled to recourse upon a petition of right to the Exchequer Court, and it has jurisdiction to determine that question as well as any other. But assuming that there may be more difficulty than I see in enforcing the right, it does not seem to me that is a conclusive reason why wp should create rights for people for which they have no claim whatsoever, simply because, if we do not, perhaps there wili be somebody who will claim them, and succeed in evading the law, or somebody who may have difficulty in showing he comes within the law.

Might I suggest to the minister that, as it is now II o'clock, he suspend the consideration of this Bill until to-morrow, and in the meantime he can consider the amendments offered by my hon. friend from St. Anne (Mr. Doherty), and my hon. friend from Assi-niboia (Mr. Turriff).

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no desire to force the Bill. I appreciate the importance of the suggestions made by the hon. member for St. Anne and by the hon. member for Assiniboia. But I understand that there are other amendments to be placed before the House, and I would suggest that we' spend half an hour more in hearing what other hon. gentlemen have 'to say, and what amendments they desire to make.

I believe my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has an important amendment, and the hon. member for North Ontario has an important amendment, and I suggest that these be made now in order that the minister may have time to consider them.

Before we go further with this Bill I wish to say that I am in harmony with it as it stands, though perhaps some amendments might be made to it. But I rise to refer to some implication that has been cast upon a gentleman who signed that circular, Col. Hamilton Merritt. It was suggested that he had at bottom some scheme to speculate in land grants. Now, every person who knows Col. Merritt knows very well that he is not that kind of a man. He is a man of ample means, a man of integrity, and of the highest honour, and r do not think for a moment that he would lend himself to any scheme of the kind. Everything he has done was for the purpose of aiding these men who still have their scrip, and I think it adds very little to the strength of any argument in this House against the Bill to cast reflection on the gentleman, who gave up a European tour to go at his own expense and serve his king in Africa. He is a man of considerable means, and he would not be a party to any attempt to bunco, as I may say, the Minister of the Interior into any legislation that is going to help land speculators. There is another thing that the House fails to note. I agree that the minister last year left the impression that there was not going to be any extension. Now, I am not an old parliamentarian, but I am an old enough Canadian to know that the minds of the government are never fixed on anything, and if I could find out from the government what they are going to do two years from now in regard to a certain thing, 1 could make a large sum of money. Consequently when a person asks the government what they are going to do on anything or at any time, they generally say that they have not considered it, or they have not contemplated doing that sort of thing. Sometimes when they are getting ready for an election they say they have got it under their serious consideration. Now, a question has been raised about speculators. It does seem to me that it would be almost impossible to pin a specu-Mr. G. TAYLOR.
lator on these amendments. Supposing we did pass a measure which would only have effect from now on, is it the intention to make the amendment such that the man who purchases from the veteran from now on will not be entitled to an extension for two years?	[DOT]
No.

Most of these grants are passed from hand to hand, made out in blank, payable to Bearer and without any date on them. The result would be that any speculator who owned scrip of this kind, if he had eight or ten of these blank scrips in his possession, would, in five minutes, put in the dates, and how could you prevent it? The only way you could do it would be to get the veterans who hold their scrips to return them and get new ones. Whatever strength there is in that suggestion I will leave to the judgment of the House. I think that the veterans are entitled to this extension. I have received fifty or sixty letters from individual veterans who hold their land scrip asking me to support a measure of this kind. I do not think there is any objection to it, and I think that if the House got down to the consideration of the clauses we might get to the meat of the thing much more quickly than by making speeches aimed against particular sections of the Bill, which might be construed as a general attack on the Bill.

I have an amendment that I think will not raise any of the difficulties which we have been discussing so far this evening. In the original Act of 1908, provision was made for a bounty to the South African veterans, and it was there provided that the grantee, as he was called, or his substitute, should select, enter and perform his settlement duties before a fixed time. A veteran might appoint a substitute under the original Act, but the peculiarity of the Act was that the substitute could not be an agent. He must be practically a purchaser, an assignee or transferee of the rights of the veteran, and the patent could issue only to the substitute and not to the veteran. It has happened in several cases that the veteran had become incapacitated so that he could not personally make the entry or selection. I have brought before the department one instance of that character. Mr. Smart of Toronto had become incapacitated in South Africa while on service there. On his return he suffered from rheumatism and nephritis, and he was quite incapable of going on the land and doing the settlement duties, but he is a man who hopes to go upon the land with his family and settle. He objects to being compelled to sell out. He wants no dealing with speculators; all he wants is the

privilege, if it can be called a privilege, [DOT]of putting a man on the land to do the work for him that he cannot do himself. But, instead of employing an agent or put-tin? his own servant on the land to do the work, he must do it himself, because the department says that if he is not doing it himself he must do it by a substitute and the substitute must get the patent in his own name. It seems so monstrously absurd that I can hardly explain it to intelligent people. Anybody would suppose that a man in the position of the man I refer to might beyond question employ somebody to do the work for him and take the patent in his own name. To man after man having applied to the department in Ottawa here they have said: You cannot do it, you must either go upon that land yourself or send a substitute, and if you send a substitute the patent must go to the substitute. It seems a monstrous thing to treat a deserving veteran in that way. You are giving him a bounty, you are doing something for his benefit in gratitude for what he has done, but you say to him: You are rheumatic, you cannot before the 31st December personally do settlement duty, and we will not let you do it by anybody else. If you put anybody else on the land he will get the patent and not you. It seems an absurdity that such should be possible, but it is actually the case. I placed the case of Mr. Smart in waiting before the department and I had the reply of the department that they could not meet his difficulty, that they could only deal with the man who himself makes the entry. All I propose to do is to say-and I have submitted the clause t-o the minister, and I hope he is not going to oppose it-that * the grantee may personally or by his agent appointed 'by him in that behalf in writing, and acting for him,' perform the settlement duties; that is, he may either do it by his own hand or send his own employee to do it for him. Then a veteran who wishes to sell out may do so by appointing a ' substitute,' as already provided for in the Act of 1908. This man wants no speculators. He wants to get the grant that the government has made to him, that he is entitled to, 'but he wants, because he is physically incapable of making that entry and doing the work by his own hands, the power of doing it by an agent. The department will not allow that. I hope there is no gentleman in this House Who will say that there is anything unreasonable in making the statute operative in such a way that a veteran may employ some other person to do the work, and then claim his rights.

I have already spoken on the amendment and I only rise by reason of the remarks made by my hon.
friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) in which he .stated that a certain implication had been levelled by the previous speaker against Mr. W. Hamilton Merritt. Inasmuch as my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Amie (Mr. Doherty) and myself were the only parties who spoke with reference to the circular to which Mr. Merritt's name was attached, I feel that I should say something. I just wish to express my regret that before the hon. member made that remark he had not waited until he had read what I had said in 'Hansard'. I made no implication against Mr. Merritt by inference the most constrained. I do not know Mr. Merritt. I have never seen him. I did not have him in mind favourably or unfavourably, and I used no words that could be so construed. I regret that my hon. friend did not wait until he had read exactly what I said in 'Hansard' because I can assure him and the House that I made no such implication; and I am sure that Mr. Merritt, if he possesses the high mental faculty and moral standing ascribed to him by my hon. friend will certainly so understand what I said.

I said there was an implication that this was an organization that was to benefit speculators, and that the agent of this organization was around here wire-pulling with the minister. Now, knowing Colonel Hamilton Merritt as I do, I do not believe he would be a party to anything of that kind for a minute.
I hope the hon. gentleman does not think I made any such imputation?
I do not think you did.
I certainly had no idea of it.

There is a big difference between the actual veteran and the speculator. For my part, I am in favour of a year's extension to the veterans, but I also wish to go on record that I shall never vote for any extension for the speculator. So far as the speculator is concerned', I will not grant him one minute more time. I have lived in the west as long as have the majority of members in this House who come from the west, and I am opposed to the speculator from beginning to end. That the speculators have retarded progress and settlement in the west every one knows. The question has been well placed before the House by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie and by the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) in that this parliament is granting to the speculator more than he expected and more than he paid for. There was no arrangement made between the veteran selling his grant and

the speculator that he would have a year longer, but nevertheless parliament steps in and says: You have bought this South African grant from the man who actually
earned it, and now we will give you another year to work on it. I won't support it.

There has been a good deal of discussion on this question which I asked a year ago. When I asked the question a year ago, it was because I heard there was going to be just such an extension of time granted by the govern-met as is now proposed. At that time the scrip was worth about $800, and when I received the answer from the minister that there was not going to be any change made at all, the price of the scrip went gradually down until about a month or so ago it was only worth $500.
Where does the hon. gentleman get his quotation?
From the grain exchange in the city of Winnipeg, and scrip wa3 sold in that city as low as $400.
To my knowledge the price in western Canada has never been under $625.
I know it has been lower than that in western Canada, and right here in the city as well.
And in Toronto.
And many of them less than $500.

Yes. But the moment it was known that this Bill was go-, ing to be introduced, the price went up to $800, and the speculative price to-day is from $800 to $900. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that the people of western Canada are against this Bill from start to finish. The grain growers at Prince Albert passed a very strong resolution against it. All the grain growers1 associations throughout western Canada are against it, because it retards the settlement of that country. The fact is there has been scrip issued by this government covering over 2,000,000 acres, and less than ten per cent of that is settled by_ actual volunteers who went to South Africa. I am decidedly against the extension of this time to the speculators, but ! will support my hon. friend from St. Boniface in his proposal that an extension should he given to the men who actually went to South Africa.
Would the hon. gentleman mind telling me how the extension of time for a year retards settlement?
Surely the hon. gentleman does not want an answer to that question?
I do.
Why, if the time is not extended, all this land will be settled before next fall, and if it is extended, settlement will be held back for another year. That's why.

As the intention to-night is merely to submit proposals for amendment, I shall not now take up the time of the House in discussing the question in detail. I may say as to this circular sent out in Colonel Merritt's name, that the names of the committee at the head of the circular which was read by the minister are no indication that any one of these gentleman ever saw the resolution or ever heard of it. As a matter of fact, it is a matter of physical impossibility that they all could have seen it, because some of them live on the Atlantic coast and some on the Pacific, and there is no evidence that they did see it. I have received circulars from gentlemen in Toronto-I will not call them speculators, but they are land agents and very decent fellows-asking in the interest of the volunteer who has already sold that the time be extended, and they tell me that a lot of the poor volunteers have already bought the scrip back from the speculators and are wanting an extension.
I suppose the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) admits that Colonel Merritt, who sent out that circular, knew what was in it. I have received a personal letter from Colonel Merritt in connection with it.

I am not at all
referring to Colonel Merritt. Colonel Merritt is a very fine gentleman.
If he signed it, you would think it would be genuine and that you could depend on it.

So far as Colonel Merritt is concerned, it is genuine enough, but the circular is presented here to influence the House and to make us believe that the gentlemen whose names are on the top of the circular, signed it. We have a perfect right to discuss that circular without referring at all to the gentlemen whose names are printed on top of it. We can do that without any disrespect to Colonel Merritt, who is a very fine fellow, or to the others.
Will the hon. gentleman let me ask him a question?
With great pleasure.
How do you know that the gentlemen whose names are signed to that circular did not know about it?
In the first place these gentlemen did not sign the circular; their names are printed at the head.
How do you know they did'nt see the circular?
It is a physical impossibility that they could have read the circular.
That would mean that there was a misrepresentation on the part of Colonel Merritt.
Nothing of the kind. If you look at the circular you will see that the names of these gentlemen are merely printed at the head of it, and there is nothing to say that they ever signed it or saw it.
That is a charge that must involve the honour of these gentlemen.
There is no question of the honour of these gentlemen about it in any sense, and I object to the interruption.
I would like to inform the hon. gentleman.
I don't wish to be interrupted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Currie) has no right to interrupt without the permission of the gentleman who has the floor.

The question of honour was dragged in by the hon. member for North Simcoe when there was no necessity for it at all. Are we going to let that circular go on record as an argument for giving the speculator an extension of time, because the member for North Simcoe says that somebody's honour is involved? I will not for one.

The hon. member has said that these gentlemen did not know anything about the circular, and I may say that I presented a petition to this House on behalf of one-half of these gentlemen in favour of the principle involved in that circular.

I do not want to
be interrupted by the hon. member.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Currie) cannot interrupt.

At the proper time,
I will propose an amendment to this effect:
The provisions of this Act, and of the Volunteer Bounty Act of 1908, shall apply to any volunteer whose domicile was in Canada at the time of the openiug of the war, and who produces indubitable evidence of his service in the field in South Africa, although he may not have been duly sworn in and enlisted.
My objection in this is to meet a number of cases that I think should be covered. The case of the doctors who went out and did splendid service will be covered by another amendment. Then, I wish to mention the case of a lad named' Devine, from Halifax, who went out in one of the corps under Capt. Beardmore. He was too young when he started to be enrolled; but he served all through South Africa, wore the Uniform, answered the roll-call every day; but owing to the fact that he was not technically enlisted and properly sworn in, he is not entitled to the benefit of the Bounty Act.

The circular read by the minister was one dated the 18th of April, 1910. The circular and correspondence to which I have referred was some months earlier. The circular which the minister tead is signed Wm. Hamilton Merritt, lieutenant colonel, secretary, and the names of the committee are at the beginning of the circular. The association is not speci-'*fically named in the circular, but I think it is of some importance to the committee to know whether this circular is authentic tor not. I assume that it is authentic, and that it expresses the views of the officers 'whose names are at the head of it. I assume also that the secretary had instructions to send that circular, and I -think this committee might very well be guided by what that circular contains. If any one makes the imputation that the circular is not authentic, I think we should have some definite information on that point. I for one shall take it as authentic, and shall be guided by its contents.

The hon. gentleman and the hon. member for North Simcoe are the only ones I have heard to-night throw any discredit on the circular. I shall deal with that matter to-morrow on its merits, and not on any ideas that may be promulgated for the extension of the Act for the benefit of the purchasers.

In regard to the circular, I _ understand that there was a South African committee appointed some years ago, and this is no doubt the same committee whose names are at the head of this circular, which was sent out by the secretary and no doubt expressed only his own personal views. No doubt the members of that committee aTe in favour of the Bill, as we are, in a restricted form. I Understood that this Bill was on behalf of men who performed a service to the country, South African veterans, but not for speculators.
How are you going to *draw the line?
It can be very easily drawn; make them produce their scrip and have it certified by the department.
Take the case mentioned by the hon. member who moved the amendment. There are hundreds of such cases.

In reference to that specific case, the young man is now in the west farjning, and., being right on the ground, he can surely locate his land before December, 1910. I have an amendment which I submitted to the minister some time ago, enlarging the scope of the Act. There were certain civil surgeons who served in the war, who were in active operations in the field with the Canadian forces, and endured all the hardships; and if any persons who were not properly enlisted are entitled to the benefits of the Act, I think 'they were. If the benefits of the Act are to include nurses, I think surgeons should also be included. Then, there were certain volunteers who died on their way to South Africa. My amendment includes them, so that the scrip will go to their heirs. The effect of my amendment is very limited; it does not extend to more than eight or ten men; but if the minister wishes to do substantial justice to the men who served in South Africa, he should accept this amendment, and I commend it to his. favourable consideration. I understand that under the regulations of the department existing at the time this Act first passed, the members of the families of two of those who idied on the way to South Africa did receive scrip. My amendment is only to make the Act general in that respect. It reads as follows:
Section 2, subsection 2 shall le amended by adding thereto the following words, viz.:
Canadian civil surgeons who served in South Africa during the war, and persons enrolled with any Canadian corps proceeding to South Africa on active service, and who died before such corps reached its destination.

When we come to deal with the Bill clause by clause, I wish to move an amendment which will be number six of the present Act changing section 2 of the original Act. It is meant to cover such cases as those who enlisted for South Africa, and received injuries while on duty which caused them to be invalided home, before they reached South Africa. I have just a few words in clause 2, that I wish to be inserted; in the 5th line after the word ' Africa,' I would insert the words ' Or began the journey thereto,' and in the 6th line after the word ' War,' there might be added ' or injuries received on the journey.' That is the change I suggest, and it will make this difference that all the men who enlisted, and entered upon their duties, but who received injuries while on duty and were invalided home would receive the privileges of the Act to which I think they are entitled just as much as the men who went to the front, in many cases much more so, because some of the men invalided home are still unfit to earn a livelihood for themselves. I do not think there are many cases, there is only one or two to my Mr. CONMEE.
knowledge in the whole Dominion]. Of course, this amendment will also cover the oases of those who died._on the journey. That is all I wish to say until we come to deal with the Bill clause by clause.

This is a favourable time to make propositions, and amendments to the Bill which we have before us. Last session I think I asked the Minister of the Interior to take into consideration the case of the men who garrisoned Halifax, and enabled the imperial troops to go to South Africa. These men enlisted, and were liable to be called at any moment to the front; in fact they were desirous of being called to South Africa, but they were not permitted to go there. I would urge the Minister of the Interior to take this matter up in connection with this Bill so that we will have the Bill made perfect. I think that last session the minister was good enough to tell me that he would bring the matter before the attention of his colleagues in the government so that I hope that when the Bill comes back he will have an amendment to the effect I have suggested, for I would rather it came from him as I know it would be more likely to go through.

As the hour of twelve o'clock has now arrived, and as I presume the minister has heard all the suggestions he wants to hear to-night, we may adjourn, and he will be able to bring a perfect Bill before us at another time.
If none of those amendments are intended to be moved to section 1, perhaps section I should pass.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I intended to say that it was only at the invitation of the minister that these amendments should be made at this stage, and none of them are to section 1, and none >are before the House at the moment. Yney will appear in ' Hansard,' and will have to be moved when the Bill comes up again.
Section 1 might pass, if the amendments proposed are to section 4.
The second jone deals with section 3 of the Act, and my amendment deals with section 2, consequently mine would come in prior to this section.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am quite willing to accept the suggestion of the member for Leeds, but if there are any other gentlemen who have an amendment in mind or a suggestion to make, I thought perhaps we might get it to-night, and it would appear in ' Hansard,' as the Chairman has said. It would be convenient for reference and might 'shorten the discussion on a future occasion. If there is no other proposition .to be placed before the House, however, I

would move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.

Motion agreed to.
Mr. PATERSON moved the adjournment of the House.
Before the House adjourns will the hon. minister say what business will be taken up to-morrow?
We will take some of the Bills that are upon the order paper, and then Supply.

I understood there was an arrangement between the leader of the opposition and the Prime Minister that we would take Supply early, because an hon. member on this side of the House has something to say. I think there is an arrangement to that effect.

I think there has been notice of -a motion that will be made on going into Supply, but I think perhaps that in the forenoon we might take up some Bills that we are anxious to get through, and send to the other Chamber.
Some non-contentious ones?
There are one or two I think that are non-contentious, and they may be taken up first.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12 o'clock (midnight.)
Wednesday, ApriJ 27, 1910.
